question: Opponent plays Fizz Trickstarter. I want to play Disposal Order. When can I respond? When opp plays Fizz or when he chooses a card to play from trash? And what next? I play Disposal Order and he chooses another cards?
answer:
You respond when Fizz's "When you play me" trigger goes on the Chain — that's the moment your opponent declares which spell in their trash Fizz will play (FAQ #10020, #12050).

You could technically also fire Disposal Order while Fizz is still a pending card on the Chain (it's a Reaction, so Closed State is fine), but at that point the trash target hasn't been chosen yet, so you'd be guessing — and you'd be wasting your spell if they pick a different card.

When your Disposal Order resolves, you pick the up to 3 cards from their trash — not them. So you recycle the targeted spell (plus up to 2 others of your choice), and when Fizz's ability resolves it finds no valid target, so the "play that spell" instruction is ignored and nothing is played (Rule 359.3.e.7). The opponent can't swap in a different target — targets are locked when the trigger was placed on the Chain.

question: If I soul harvest an enemy unit in a battlefield in which I have no units on, can my opponent play an ambush card to put that unit into the battlefield?
answer:
Yes — your opponent can play an Ambush unit to that battlefield in reaction to Soul Harvest.

Soul Harvest on the chain creates a Closed State, and since your opponent still controls the targeted unit at that battlefield, Ambush's condition is met: they may play a unit there and gain [Reaction] timing for that play (Rule 822.1.b). The Ambush unit finalizes and enters play immediately — you get no window to react to the unit play itself (FAQ #9326) — and then Soul Harvest resolves and kills the targeted unit. The Ambush unit stays, so your opponent keeps presence at that battlefield.

The only catch: they have to play it while the unit is still there. If they wait until after Soul Harvest resolves and the unit is dead, there are no units at the location and Ambush's permission no longer applies (Rule 822.3).

question: Can I use 2 more reactions at once?
answer:
Yes. Priority doesn't leave you until you choose to pass it, so you can play as many Reactions as you can afford in a row (Rule 312; FAQ #4744).

A few notes:

You pay each cost as the card is put on the chain, not as it resolves.

Everything resolves last-in-first-out (your second Reaction resolves before your first, then the original spell/ability).

After each one resolves, priority is offered again — so your opponent gets chances to respond in between resolutions.

This only works for cards/abilities that are legally timed in a Closed State (i.e., they have Reaction). Regular Actions need an Open State with an empty chain.

question: When Red Akali moves into a battlefield where Blue Teemo is defending, does Teemo's "When I defend" go on the chain first, or can Akali instantly use her Legend ability and move Red Akali unit back as an action?
answer:
No — Teemo's "When I defend" goes on the Chain first; you can't use the legend ability to preempt it.

Here's the order: Akali's "When I move" resolves first (dealing 1, or 2 if Empowered — if that kills Teemo, there's no Showdown at all and no defend trigger). After that chain empties, a Cleanup stages the Showdown: Teemo gains the Defender designation and his "When I defend" is placed on the Chain immediately (Rule 383.3) — there's no priority window in between.

While that trigger is on the Chain the state is Closed, and only Reaction-speed effects can be played. The Rogue Assassin legend ability is [Action], so it can't be used as a response (Rules 145.2, 381). Your first chance to move Akali back is after Teemo's trigger resolves and the Chain empties back to Showdown Open State — at that point you can activate the legend ability, move Akali to base, and the Showdown unstages before combat damage (FAQ #11755).

question: If I'm defending with Ravenbloom Student at the Battlefield Fortified Position, and my opponent comes in with Akali Deadly Weapon, activates the legend ability of Akali and moves Akali Deadly Weapon out, does my Ravenbloom Student survive from the Fortified Position shield proc? Or does Ravenbloom Student die from the 2 damage dealt to it?
answer:
No — Ravenbloom Student dies from the 2 damage. Fortified Position's "When you defend here" Shield never procs, because the Student is killed in the Cleanup before Combat is ever staged, so it never becomes the Defender.

Here's the order: Akali moves in → Contested applies → Cleanup runs → her "When I move" trigger resolves, dealing 2 to the Student (2 Might, 2 damage = lethal). In the next Cleanup, the Student is killed in step 3b (CR 323.4) — which happens before step 7 (CR 323.8) checks for opposing units to stage Combat. With only Akali remaining, no Combat stages, the Student never gains the Defender designation, and Fortified Position's condition ("When you defend here") is never met.

The Rogue Assassin legend move-out changes nothing: it's an [Action] ability requiring an Open State and a unit already in a showdown, so it can't happen until after the Showdown is staged — which is after the Student is already in the trash. (This matches FAQ #11762 and #11827: Akali's move damage lands before any Shield/defend trigger can apply.)

question: Can I play Star Crossed as a reaction to an empower ability?
answer:
Yes. Empower is an activated ability (Rule 827), so it goes on the Chain as a Pending item and creates a Closed State (Rule 377.3). Star-Crossed has [Reaction], so you can play it during that Closed State.

The key timing: Star-Crossed resolves first (LIFO), before the Empower completes — so the unit isn't Empowered yet and any [Empowered][>] ability isn't active. If you bounce the unit to hand, the Empower does nothing when it resolves.

One requirement: you need both a friendly unit and an enemy unit on the board to target (Star-Crossed requires one of each).

question: When you play Temporal Breach on a battlefield you control, does it start a showdown?
answer:
No — if the unit's owner already controls the battlefield, no showdown starts.

Temporal Breach banishes a unit and its owner plays it back to the same location. Contested is only applied when a unit becomes present at a battlefield its controller doesn't already control (Rule 190.3.a.1). Replaying your own unit to a battlefield you control doesn't satisfy that, so nothing is staged (matches FAQ #8066 — playing a unit to a battlefield you control never triggers a showdown).

One caveat: if you target an opponent's unit sitting on a battlefield you control, the opponent plays their unit back to a battlefield they don't control — that applies Contested and a showdown (combat or non-combat, depending on who else has units there) will be staged in the next cleanup.

question: Does Applied Researcher affect repeat costs?
answer:
Yes — once she's Empowered, Applied Researchers' discount applies to Repeat costs too.

Repeat is an optional additional cost that gets added to the spell's total cost during finalization (Rule 356.2), and her "your spells cost [1] [A] less" is a total-cost discount applied after all costs are summed (Rule 356.4). So a spell that costs [2] plus a [Repeat] [2] cost totals 4, and you'd pay 3 (FAQ #11935). The discount applies once to the combined total — it does not reduce each Repeat execution separately — and the "minimum of [1]" only caps her Energy discount, never prevents it.

question: Does Vi Peacekeepers still stun if she gets bounced and no longer at that battlefield?
answer:
No — if Vi is bounced before her attack trigger resolves, the stun fizzles.

Her ability reads "When I attack, [Stun] an enemy unit here." The word "here" requires Vi herself to still be at that battlefield when the ability resolves. If she's returned to hand (e.g., Star-Crossed or Flash) in response to the trigger, the chain resolves last-in-first-out — the bounce resolves first, and when her trigger tries to resolve it can't reference her location, so no unit gets stunned (FAQ #10045, #10627). Same applies if she's killed instead of bounced.

question: I play Imperial Decree, can I use my 2 Might unit to kill a 2M backline unit and 4M unit of opponent?
answer:
No — you can't kill both. Your 2 Might only reaches the 4M unit, so the 2M Backline unit survives untouched.

Damage assignment requires lethal damage to one unit before moving to the next (CR 467.2.c.3), and Backline makes the 2M unit an invalid target until every non-Backline defender has lethal damage assigned (Rule 826.4.b). Your 2 points must all go to the 4M unit — not enough to kill it normally, but Imperial Decree's trigger kills it the moment it takes damage. The Backline unit takes 0 damage and lives.

Meanwhile the defenders assign 6 back, so your 2M unit dies too. To use Decree against Backline, you need to attack in separate showdowns, one unit at a time (see FAQ 5012).

question: If I burn cards and I burn Flame Chompers, can I play it for through its effect?
answer:
No. Burning Flame Chompers does not trigger its ability — "discard" only means hand → trash (CR 423.1), while Burn moves cards from the top of your Main Deck to trash (CR 441.1). They're different game actions, so the "when you discard me" trigger never fires.

The card stays in your trash; you'd need a separate recursion effect to get it back. (Same reason it doesn't trigger when it's Killed.)

question: If there is damage on a unit, will it still die if I play Elder Dragon and bounce it?
answer:
Yes — the damaged enemy unit dies the moment Elder Dragon enters, and bouncing Elder Dragon afterward won't undo it.

The passive kicks in as a state check immediately upon Elder Dragon entering the battlefield: any enemy unit with even 1 of your damage marked on it becomes lethal and is killed in the cleanup that runs right away — before you even get priority to respond to the "When you play me" trigger (FAQ #10686, #11834). So there's no window to bounce Elder Dragon first and dodge the kill.

Once the death has happened, returning Elder Dragon to hand doesn't resurrect the unit — the lethality of already-marked damage doesn't retroactively disappear (FAQ #9875). Two caveats: the damage on the unit must be your damage (marked by you), and the unit must be an enemy unit. If it's your own unit, Elder Dragon's passive does nothing to it.

question: If I have Mel awakened empowered and I stupefy my own empowered Gangplank, does he only gain 1 might instead of 2 or does he get 6?
answer:
Neither — Gangplank gains +3 Might this turn, so he ends at 9 (6 base + 3). Mel's extra −1 never lands.

Empowered Mel makes Stupefy's reduction −2 (to a minimum of 1), but Stupefy chooses Gangplank, so his Empowered replacement fires: a spell that would give him −[S] instead gives him +3 [S] this turn. The entire reduction is replaced — Mel's additional −1 is not applied on top, and the "minimum of 1" floor never comes into play. If you order Mel's modification first you get "would give −2 → replaced by +3"; if you order Gangplank's replacement first, the spell no longer gives −[S], so Mel has nothing to modify — either way it's +3. Stupefy's draw still happens, and the +3 wears off at end of turn. (FAQ #11914; Rule 372.)

question: Can the list ability be reacted to?
answer:
Yes — but only the [T] activated ability, not the "as you play" naming.

The List's [T]: Give a unit with the named tag -2 [S] this turn. is an activated ability. Activated abilities go on the Chain just like a spell, which creates a Closed State and gives opponents a window to respond with Reactions (CR 377.3, 407.4). So your opponent can react to the -2 [S] before it resolves.

The "As you play this, name a tag" instruction, however, happens while playing the Gear itself — permanents finalize immediately with no Reaction window, so that part can't be responded to (Rule 9107). Timing note: the ability is still restricted to your Main Phase in an Open State unless it gains Reaction — your opponent can't fire it on your turn.

question: If my legend is Master Yi, I have a Fiora Peerless Duelist alone on a battlefield, and my opponent starts a showdown with only one unit, can I get the +2 might from Master Yi first before Fiora's might is doubled? What happens if I play a Punch first after the showdown starts? Would Fiora double that might as well?
answer:
Yes — Fiora ends at 10 Might, and no, Punch First's +5 doesn't get doubled.

Your Master Yi (Wuju Bladesman, Starter) gives a passive +2 Might the moment Fiora is designated as the lone defender, before anything hits the chain (Arithmetic layer). Fiora goes 3 → 5, then her "when I defend one on one" trigger resolves and doubles her current Might: 5 × 2 = 10, not 8.

For Punch First: it's an [Action], so you cannot play it while Fiora's trigger is on the chain — the game is Closed and only [Reaction] cards are legal (FAQ #8421). You have to wait until the chain empties, by which point her trigger has already resolved on her 5 Might. Playing Punch First then gives her +5 for a final 15 Might; the doubling does not re-apply to bonuses added afterward (CR 433.1 — doubling uses the value at the moment it resolves).

question: When Master Yi tempered attacks with 7 might to a Darius with 5 might, Draven player who has Darius reveal hidden card Switcheroo. Does the Master Yi which is at 7 might gain the might of Darius being at 5 or at 7 because he played the second card this turn?
answer:
Master Yi gains 5 — Switcheroo swaps using each unit's current Might when it resolves, and Darius is sitting at 5.

Darius's "+2 Might when you play your second card" is a triggered ability that only goes on the Chain after the card that made it your second card fully resolves (FAQ #5184). Since Switcheroo is played before any such trigger fires, the swap uses Darius's current 5: Master Yi drops to 5, Darius rises to 7.

Then, if Switcheroo was indeed your second card this turn, Darius's trigger resolves afterward: he gets +2 to 9 and readies. Either way, Master Yi keeps 5 for the rest of the turn (FAQ #7874).

question: Am I allowed to empower Matriarch of War legend with "Kayle, Justified" second and third empower?
answer:
Yes — you can activate Kayle's Empower a second and third time, and Matriarch of War's trigger fires each time — but only the first one does anything to her.

Kayle's text "I can be Empowered up to three times" is a permission that overrides the normal "can't Empower something already Empowered" restriction (CR 442.1.c.1), so the 2nd and 3rd Empower activations are legal.

Each activation is an "empower something else" event, so Matriarch of War's trigger goes on the Chain every time. But since Matriarch is already Empowered after the first one, the 2nd and 3rd triggers do nothing when they resolve — her own text says "I become Empowered if I'm not already," and Empowered is a binary state (CR 442.1.a–c). She doesn't gain extra Empower stacks; only Kayle tracks her count.

question: If I play Temporal Breach on a defender at a battlefield, when they replay, are they now the attacker?
answer:
No — the replayed unit is still the Defender, and its controller stays the Defender.

The Attacker is defined by who first applied Contested to that battlefield (CR 461.2.b) — that's the player who moved in, and Temporal Breach doesn't change it. The defender controls the battlefield even while it's contested, so playing the unit back to the same location doesn't apply a new Contested and can't flip the designations.

The banished-and-replayed unit is a new game object, so it will regain the Defender designation during the next Cleanup — which is why Ahri's "when I defend" trigger can fire again in the same combat (FAQ #5362, #11974). But it regains it as a Defender, not an Attacker.

question: Hextech Anomaly if I pay a Ready Rune to get an energy, does that mean I get 2 Fleeting Energy, one from Hextech Anomaly and the other for floating a rune?
answer:
Yes — one ready rune can give you 2 floating energy, but only if you use its Recycle ability to fuel Hextech Anomaly.

The full sequence: exhaust the ready rune for 1 Energy ([E] → Add [1]), then Recycle that same exhausted rune for 1 Power of its domain, then exhaust Hextech Anomaly, paying that 1 Power to Add 1 Energy (FAQ #164). Net result: 2 Energy floating for the turn, at the cost of the rune (recycled) and Anomaly (exhausted).

The rune itself only ever gives you 1 Energy from its tap — the second Energy comes from Anomaly converting the power you get from recycling that rune. Both float until your pool empties (end of draw phase / end of turn, Rule 167).

question: Does Ivern Friend to All get the extra point if I have units with all the different tags at the same battlefield as him, or can they be anywhere in play (e.g., bird, poro, and cat with Ivern at battlefield and dog at base)?
answer:
Yes — they can be anywhere in play under your control.

Ivern's ability says "if your units have all of the following tags among them," not "at this battlefield." So as long as you control at least one Bird, one Cat, one Dog, and one Poro across your base and all battlefields, the condition is met (FAQ #10315). A Dog at your base counts just the same as one sitting next to Ivern.

question: If opponent has Frozen Fortress and forgot to trigger the Frozen Fortress and suddenly remembered, how does judge resolve this?
answer:
It depends on when they remember — the key is whether a new game action has been taken since the trigger's observable impact point.

If a new game action has been taken (e.g., they moved to scoring, drew, played a spell/unit): the trigger is forgotten (TR 506.3.b). It never goes on the chain, so the damage is not applied retroactively (TR 506.4; FAQ #11413).

If they remember before any new game action after the Beginning Step: it's not yet forgotten — the controller can still acknowledge it and put the Frozen Fortress trigger on the chain normally.

When a judge is called on a missed trigger (TR 702.2.f):

Same turn the trigger was missed → the next opponent in turn order chooses whether to resolve the damage immediately or leave it missed (TR 702.2.f.2; FAQ #5809).

Later turn → play continues; the damage is skipped (TR 702.2.f.1).

Penalty-wise: missing a mandatory trigger is normally No Penalty, but if missing it was advantageous to the controller (e.g., it would only have damaged your units, not theirs), it's a Warning (TR 702.2.e). Frozen Fortress's damage is sourced from the battlefield, so the accountable player is whoever controls it (TR 506.1.a).

question: When you play a unit from Kharox Empower, after that played unit dies, does it go to your trash or the enemy's?
answer:
It goes to the opponent's trash — you control the unit, but they still own it.

When Kharox's Empower lets you play a unit from your opponent's trash, you gain control of it, but ownership doesn't change. If that unit is killed later, it goes to its owner's trash (Rule 56: a card can never enter a non-board zone belonging to another player, so it returns to the opponent's trash). This applies to any card you play from an opponent's trash, not just Kharox.

question: Explain to me how the interaction of Switcharoo targeting my Shadow Clone with Assault 4 has with an enemy unit with 7 might.
answer:
Yes — it fully swaps the numbers: your clone becomes 7 Might and the enemy drops to 4, with Assault staying on the clone as part of that value.

While attacking, the clone's current Might is 0 (base) + 4 (Assault) = 4. Switcheroo snapshots current Mights (4 vs 7), finds a difference of 3, and applies +3 to your clone and −3 to the enemy. Assault is not reapplied on top of the new value — it was included in the snapshot and keeps applying to its original unit (FAQ #341, same as the Assault/Shield Switcheroo precedent). So during combat: clone = 0 + 4 (Assault) + 3 = 7, enemy = 7 − 3 = 4.

Consequences: the clone deals 7 combat damage (lethal against the 4-Might enemy), while the enemy deals only 4 back — not lethal against the clone's 7. After combat ends, the clone loses Assault and drops to 3 Might (0 base + the +3 modifier, which persists until end of turn). One edge case: if you cast Switcheroo while the clone isn't attacking, its Might is 0, so the clone would gain +7 (enemy drops to 0) — and if it attacks later that turn, Assault 4 stacks on top for a total of 11.

question: How does Star Crossed work when it gets rebuttal by a Mel deck?
answer:
It depends on what you do when Rebuttal resolves — and you decide then, not when you play it.

Rebuttal (Mel's signature, [1] Mind/Chaos) can target Star-Crossed since its Energy cost of 3 is within the "no more than [4]" limit. On resolution, you either pay [A] to take control and make new choices, or decline and counter it (FAQ 12038).

If you take control, "friendly" and "enemy" re-anchor to you. Star-Crossed's two targets are both mandatory — you must pick one unit you control and one your opponent controls — so you can retarget either or both slots, but you can never bounce two of your opponent's units. If you decline the [A], Star-Crossed is simply countered and does nothing (CR 426.1).

One catch: Star-Crossed must still be on the chain when Rebuttal resolves — if it was already countered or removed, Rebuttal fizzles and you keep your runes (FAQ 12069).

question: Can I tap Irelia legend when I select her during a showdown with a spell?
answer:
Yes. Playing a spell that chooses Irelia, Fervent during a Showdown triggers Blade Dancer's ability ("When you choose a friendly unit, you may exhaust me and pay [A] to ready it"), so you can tap the Legend and pay a Rune to ready her (FAQ #9382).

Note the extra payoff: readying Irelia, Fervent also fires her own "when you ready me" trigger, stacking another +1 Might on top of the +1 she gets from being chosen. If she's already readied, the ready does nothing (CR 416.1.c), but you can still pay.

question: If I hide Zhonya and my Poro dies triggering its Deathknell, can I play Zhonya in response to the Deathknell?
answer:
Yes — you can flip Zhonya's Hourglass in response to the Deathknell trigger, but it won't save the Poro.

Hidden cards gain Reaction when played from facedown (Rule 811), and the Deathknell trigger going on the chain puts the game in a Closed State — so you have a window to play it. However, Zhonya's is a replacement effect ("if a friendly unit would die"), so it has to be active before the death happens. By the time the Deathknell trigger is on the chain, the Poro has already died and been sent to trash (Rule 808.1.d.2), so the Zhonya's enters too late to replace anything. It'll hit the board as gear, and the Deathknell still resolves — you draw 1 if the Poro died alone.

One caveat: this reaction window exists because Deathknell formed the chain (and battlefields stay locked during an ongoing Combat). If the Poro died with no trigger to react to, cleanup would discard your hidden Zhonya's before you got a chance to flip it.

question: Do units heal after Showdown? Open Showdown and Combat Showdown?
answer:
No — it depends on whether the showdown is a combat showdown or not.

Combat Showdown (Contested battlefield with units from opposing players): yes. After combat damage, Combat Cleanup heals all units in play — every unit everywhere, whether or not it fought (CR 463.1.a.1).

Non-Combat Showdown (Contested battlefield where only one player has units): no healing. There's no Combat Cleanup after a non-combat showdown, so units stay damaged until the end of turn cleanup (Rule 344.2).

Separately, all units still heal all damage at the end of each player's turn (Rule 317.2.b), so damaged units won't stay hurt forever.

question: What is the difference between killing Poro with Hidden Zhonya in the Showdown and outside Showdown?
answer:
The difference is when your last chance to flip Zhonya's happens — and whether it can actually save the Poro.

In the Combat Showdown: once both players pass, the Showdown Closes and damage is assigned and dealt with no window for reactions (CR 467.2). The Poro dies during Combat Cleanup. By the time its Deathknell opens a reaction window, the death has already happened — and Zhonya's is a replacement effect that must be active before the death to replace it (Rule 369.1). So a still-hidden Zhonya's cannot save the Poro from combat damage. Your only shot is flipping it during the Showdown Open State, before you pass — which reveals it and lets your opponent assign damage accordingly. (Flipping it in the Deathknell window still saves the Zhonya's itself from being trashed if you lose control of the battlefield.)

Outside the showdown: if the Poro is killed by a spell or ability on the chain, that creates a Closed State — you can flip the hidden Zhonya's as a Reaction before the kill resolves. When the kill lands, Zhonya's is face-up and active, so it replaces the death: Zhonya's is killed instead, the Poro is healed, exhausted, and recalled to base, and no Deathknell triggers. The one exception is a death that happens during a cleanup with no prior chain window (e.g., lethal damage already marked) — there you're too late either way.

question: Why can't you save Zhonya when opponent kill my poro with desthknell outside showdown?
answer:
You can flip Zhonya's in response to the Deathknell trigger outside a Showdown, but it won't save the Poro — the death has already happened by then.

Zhonya's is a replacement effect ("if a friendly unit would die, kill this instead") and it only applies at the exact instant the death event occurs. When the opponent's kill resolves, the Poro is dead and in the trash, and its Deathknell trigger is just the result of that death hitting the chain. There's no longer a death event to replace, so flipping Zhonya's now only gets it onto the board.

The real window to save the Poro is earlier: react to the kill spell itself with your hidden Zhonya's before it resolves. If you do, the death is replaced with heal/exhaust/recall, the Poro lives, and Deathknell never triggers (Rule 808.1.d.1). Reaction timing works identically inside and outside Showdowns — any Closed State is fine.

question: When do I have to trash my hidden card? After showdown end or after my only unit killed?
answer:
It depends on whether a Showdown is still running.

Your hidden card trashes when you lose control of the battlefield (CR 323.6.a). That timing changes based on context:

Outside a Showdown/Combat (Open State, no chain): the moment your last unit is killed, you lose control in the following cleanup and the hidden card goes to the trash — there's no window to flip it (CR 187.4.c, 323.5).

During a Showdown/Combat: the battlefield is Contested, so you keep control even with zero units. Your hidden card stays put and you can still flip it as a Reaction. It only trashes when the Showdown fully resolves and you still control no units there (CR 468.5.c).

One caveat: if a Deathknell or other trigger from your dying unit creates a chain, that opens a window to play the hidden card before control is lost. Otherwise, outside of combat, a killed last unit is "checkmate" for your hidden.

question: Can an enemy Disposal Orders my trash before I choose to play something from my trash with Fizz?
answer:
They can't force you to choose first and then strike in a "blind" window — but the practical answer is yes, they can still stop Fizz. Here's the timing:

When Fizz's "When you play me" trigger goes on the Chain, that's the exact moment you pick the spell in your trash (FAQ #10020). There's no gap where your choice is pending — you declare the target as you add the trigger, and that choice locks it in.

What your opponent can do:

After you've declared your target (the normal play): they respond to Fizz's trigger with Disposal Order, recycle the targeted spell, and Fizz's ability fizzles — with no valid target, the "play that spell" instruction is ignored (Rule 359.3.e.7; FAQ #10771). The spell never gets played.

While Fizz is still pending on the Chain (before his trigger even exists): Disposal Order is a Reaction, so it's legal, but they're guessing — you haven't chosen yet, so they'd be wasting it if you pick a different card.

So they can't snipe your choice before it exists, but once you name the card, Disposal Order in response makes Fizz do nothing. Your only real protection is having the spell be un-recyclable or answering their Disposal Order first.

question: When I play Astral Heron to a battlefield, does my next card this turn get reduced by 2 energy and 2 power?
answer:
Yes — if Astral Heron is the first card you play that turn, your next card costs [2] Energy and [A][A] (2 Power, any domain) less.

Heron counts as your first card; once it's finalized at a battlefield, its trigger sees that condition satisfied and fires — the discount then applies to the next (second) card you play. It never discounts itself.

Caveat: if you already played another card earlier that turn, Heron won't trigger — the "first card" event already passed, and Heron wasn't at a battlefield when it was evaluated (FAQ #11863, #11952).

question: If I use Facebraker in a battlefield where I have a unit, can I play it without an enemy in there?
answer:
No. Facebreaker requires both a friendly unit and an enemy unit at the same battlefield as valid targets when you play it — you can't play it with only your own unit present (RiftJudge FAQ #40).

The "stun a friendly unit and an enemy unit" wording is a group targeting requirement, so the play is illegal and cancelled if either target is missing. Having just a friendly unit isn't enough.

question: Can I play 1 energy to give Renekton, Brute 1 might on the enemy turn?
answer:
No. Renekton, Brute's ability [1]: Give me +1 [M] this turn is a standard activated ability with no Reaction tag, so it can only be activated on your own turn, during your Main Phase, in an Open State (Rules 145.2, 381). On your opponent's turn you have no such window for it.

The only thing that can fire on the enemy turn is his triggered ability ("When my Might becomes 10 or more, empower me") — but you can't manually pay the 1 Energy to make that happen off-turn.

question: If I move a unit into a contested battlefield and activate a move trigger, can I reaction speed a spell to move out of the battlefield before combat starts?
answer:
Yes — if the move trigger opens a chain, you can play a Reaction-speed spell to move the unit out before the showdown starts, and the combat won't happen.

The move trigger creates a chain (Neutral Closed State), and during a Closed State only Reaction spells/abilities can be played (Rule 813). That window is your only chance: once the chain empties, a Cleanup runs and the staged Combat opens immediately with no priority for non-Reaction play (FAQ #1645, #3814).

If your Reaction moves the unit away, the Combat ceases being Staged (CR 323.9 / 461.2) and Contested is removed in the next Cleanup since you no longer have units there (CR 323.10) — so no Showdown or Combat ever begins. Two caveats: your move trigger still resolves, but any "here"-dependent instructions on it will fail since you're gone (Rule 359.3.e.12), and if the unit has no move trigger, there's no chain at all and you get no window to react before combat starts.

question: If I have a Ahri Nine Tailed Fox Legend and the enemy attacks a battlefield with Assault, does the effect from Ahri apply before or after the Assault effect?
answer:
Yes — Assault applies first, then Ahri's -1 Might.

Assault is a passive ability that takes effect the moment the unit gains the Attacker designation, before any triggers go on the chain. Ahri's Nine-Tailed Fox ability then triggers on that designation and resolves afterward, reducing the already-buffed Might. So a 3-Might unit with Assault 3 attacks at 6 Might, then Ahri brings it to 5. This matches FAQ 213 and Rule 807.1.c (Assault is a passive, not a trigger).

question: What is considered as win a combat?
answer:
You win a combat if you are the Attacker or Defender and you are the only player with units still at that battlefield when combat result is determined (CR 468.3.a).

Damage doesn't have to happen — you win even if the opponent's units were bounced, killed, or moved away during the Showdown, as long as only your units remain. Three exceptions produce "No Result" where nobody wins: attackers were Recalled during Combat Cleanup (even if only defenders remain), both players still have units, or neither player has units. Also note conquering an empty battlefield is not winning a combat — no combat occurred (FAQ #9092).

question: If the opponent enters my battlefield with a unit that says "when I attack" but in the same battlefield I have a unit that says "when I defend", which one procs first?
answer:
The "When I defend" trigger resolves first — even though the "When I attack" trigger goes on the chain first.

Here's why: when combat opens, the attacker (who applied Contested and has Focus) puts their "when I attack" triggers on the chain first, and the defender puts "when I defend" triggers on last. Since the chain resolves last-in-first-out, the defender's trigger resolves first, then the attacker's.

So: "procs" (goes on chain) = attacker first; "resolves" = defender first. (CR 466.2.d.1, Rule 340.1)

question: Can Kennen give Flow for a spell got discarded by Minefield when conquering with Kennen?
answer:
No. Kennen's target is locked when his conquer trigger is placed on the Chain, and at that moment Minefield hasn't resolved yet — so the cards it mills into your trash aren't there to choose.

Both "when you conquer" triggers go on the Chain at the same time (Rules 383.3–383.4), and targets for triggered abilities are chosen at finalization, not resolution (Rule 352.4.b). You can order Minefield first and Kennen second, but Kennen already locked his target before Minefield resolves — so the top 2 cards from Minefield are never eligible.

Side note: Minefield's mill isn't a Discard game action either, so it won't trigger "when you discard" effects. To use Kennen on a milled spell, you'd need that spell in your trash before the conquer happens — e.g., mill first, conquer later.

question: Does defying or playing a rebuttal on a spell played from flow still banish the spell?
answer:
Yes — a countered Flow spell is still banished, but only when it's actually countered.

Flow's banishment is a delayed replacement effect (Rule 829.1.b.1): any time the spell leaves the chain as a finalized chain item — except by resolving on its own — it's banished instead of trashed. A counter (Defy, or Rebuttal's "otherwise, counter it" branch) sends it to banishment, not to the trash. The counter also means "when you play" triggers won't fire and costs aren't refunded.

One exception: if Rebuttal's controller pays [A] and takes control instead of countering, the spell isn't countered — it resolves and then goes to its owner's trash normally, since leaving the chain was instructed by its own execution. (Rule 829.1.b.1, FAQ #11690)

question: At Battlefield A, my opponent controls 2 units (Mystic Poro and Sinister Poro) and I control 1 unit (Lonely Poro) along with a face-down Hidden Lotus Trap. If combat happens and I activate Hidden Lotus Trap targeting the opponent's Mystic Poro, how does the combat resolve and what is the exact outcome?
answer:
All three units die — it's a full trade — and you draw 1 from Lonely Poro's Deathknell. No one scores; Battlefield A becomes Uncontrolled.

You're the defender (your Hidden card means you controlled the battlefield), so your opponent is the attacker with 3 total Might (Mystic 2 + Sinister 1) vs. your 2 Might.

Their assignment: 2 damage to your Lonely Poro = lethal on its 2 Might.

Your assignment: With Lotus Trap active on Mystic Poro, you assign only 1 damage to Mystic (it doubles to 2, lethal on 2 Might) and 1 damage to Sinister (lethal on 1 Might). CR 467.2.c.5 factors Lotus Trap's doubling into the assignment itself, so you don't need to "spend" 2 damage to kill Mystic.

All damage is dealt simultaneously — all three units die. Lonely Poro died alone (no other friendly units there), so its Deathknell triggers and you draw 1. Combat result is No Result (no units remain), and per CR 468.5.b the battlefield becomes Uncontrolled.

One caveat: Sinister Poro's attack trigger lets your opponent pay [1] to move your Lonely Poro to its base before damage — if they do, the combat never reaches a damage step and Mystic Poro survives while they establish control.

question: Does Applied Researchers reduce repeat costs?
answer:
Yes — once Applied Researchers is Empowered, her "your spells cost [1] [A] less" discount applies to Repeat costs too.

Repeat is an optional additional cost that gets added to the spell's total cost during finalization (Rule 356.2), and her discount is a total-cost discount applied after all costs are summed (Rule 356.4). So a spell costing [2] with a [Repeat] [2] cost totals 4, and you'd pay 3.

The discount applies once to the combined total — it doesn't reduce each Repeat execution separately — and the "to a minimum of [1]" only caps her Energy discount, so it never prevents the reduction.

question: When Lucian Gunslinger attacks and there is only 1 deflect unit there, can he pass his ability or does he have to do it?
answer:
He can't skip it outright, but he can get out of it by declining the Deflect cost.

Lucian's "When I attack" trigger is mandatory (no "may"), so it goes on the Chain as a Pending Item. If the Deflect unit is the only enemy unit there, he must choose it as the target (CR 403.4) — that's not optional. However, Deflect imposes a Mandatory Additional Cost, and at the Pay Costs step he may decline to pay it (CR 405.2). If he declines, the trigger is removed from the Chain and never resolves — no damage.

Net result: he can effectively "pass" on the damage, but the trigger still appears and the Deflect unit must be chosen first. (CR 405.2)

question: If my Forerunner dies and I am playing Rengar Pridestalker, do the tokens summoned from Forerunner give plus 1 to other units?
answer:
Yes. Each Mech token is "played" when Forerunner's Deathknell resolves, so Pridestalker triggers once per token — two triggers, each giving a unit +1 Might (not one +2).

You can put both +1s on the same unit or split them between two units. Since the tokens are played to your base, they're also legal targets for the bonus themselves if you want (the ability says "a unit," not "another unit").

question: Does Ravenbloom Conservatory make you reveal to opponent?
answer:
Yes — "reveal" means the card is shown to all players, including your opponent.

Ravenbloom Conservatory's ability uses the game action Reveal, which per CR 425.1 is "presenting a card to all players" — so the top card of your Main Deck becomes public information during the resolution, then either goes to your hand or gets recycled. The effect is mandatory too: no "may," so you can't decline to reveal (FAQ #8464).

question: If I have 2 or more units with Tank on a battlefield and the opponent is trying to conquer it, can I decide which of my units gets the damage first, then second, etc.?
answer:
No — the attacker decides, not you.

During the Combat Damage step, the attacking player assigns their damage and chooses which of your Tank units takes lethal damage first when you have multiple Tanks at the battlefield. Since your Tanks share the same damage-assignment priority, the attacker may assign to them in any order (CR 815.1.c.2, 467.2.c.7). All your Tanks must still be assigned lethal damage before any non-Tank units of yours can be assigned damage.

question: If I swap Zed with a shadow clone, does a targeted spell still hit Zed or hit the clone?
answer:
The spell still hits Zed — the Shadow Clone is never the target.

Targeting locks onto the game object (Zed), not his location. When he swaps places with the clone, the targeting relationship follows Zed across the board (same principle as the Alpha Strike clarification: the "arrow" stays on the unit as long as it remains on the board). The clone was never chosen, so it can't become the spell's target.

What actually matters is whether Zed still meets the spell's targeting restrictions at resolution (Rule 359.3.e.5). If the spell just needs "a unit" and he merely moved battlefield-to-battlefield, he's still legal and takes the effect. But if the spell required him to be at a specific battlefield or in combat (e.g., Hidden Blade, or a "unit in combat" requirement), Zed is no longer a legal target after the swap — the spell misses and does nothing to the clone either.

One timing note: Zed's swap is an [Action] ability, so it can't be activated in direct response to a spell already on the Chain (that's Closed State, Reaction only). It only works in Open State — your Main Phase, or mid-combat during Showdown Open.

question: Can Baron Nashor be targeted by an enemy Battlefield effect, i.e. Amateur Recital that's controlled by an enemy?
answer:
No — an enemy-controlled Amateur Recital cannot target Baron Nashor.

Baron's ability says he can't be chosen by enemy spells and abilities, and a battlefield's ability is controlled by its controller (Rule 190.6.a). Since the enemy controls Amateur Recital, its hold trigger is an enemy ability, and choosing which unit to move to its base counts as "choosing" that unit for targeting purposes — the word "choose" doesn't need to appear on the card. That makes Baron an illegal choice (RiftJudge FAQ #8771; Rules 355.9.b, 355.10).

This is true regardless of which battlefield the units are on — the battlefield's controller, not the battlefield's owner, determines whose ability it is. If you controlled Amateur Recital, you could move your own Baron, since it would be a friendly ability.

question: Does the effect of Mask Mother count as an additional cost and is reduced by Ezreal?
answer:
No. Mask Mother's ability is a triggered ability with a cost within instructions ("you may pay [1] to give +2 [S]"), not an optional additional cost, so Ezreal, Prodigy's discount does not apply.

Ezreal only reduces costs that use both "as an additional cost" and "may" (Rule 356.2.b, FAQ #8415/#9237). Mask Mother's [1] payment happens during resolution of her trigger, in the form "[do X] to [do Y]" (CR 204.3) — the same reason Ezreal can't discount abilities like Draven's attack/defend cost. Even though it says "may," it's not an "additional cost" to play anything, so the [1] stays full price.

question: Does Overzealous Fan stop "when I attack" units effects from resolving when he uses his ability?
answer:
No — the attack trigger still resolves; Overzealous Fan doesn't cancel it.

The "When I attack" ability was already placed on the chain when the unit gained the Attacker designation (Rule 383.4.e), and the Fan's defend trigger resolves before it (defender triggers go on top, LIFO). Moving the attacker to its base does not stop its trigger from resolving.

What changes is whether the effect can actually do anything: if the trigger references "here" or otherwise needs the unit to still be at that battlefield — e.g. "deal damage to an enemy unit here" — it will fizzle, because "here" is checked on execution and now refers to the unit's base (Rule 359.3.f.2, the Yasuo/Fight or Flight example). Effects that don't depend on location or combat status (e.g. "when I attack, draw 1") resolve normally. If the attack trigger targeted the Fan specifically, that instruction is also ignored since the Fan is in the trash.

question: When you reveal a unit with Paaka Protector, does it have to go to hand or can you trash it for +2?
answer:
No — if the revealed card is a unit, you must draw it. The +2 Shield only happens when the revealed card is not a unit.

Pakaa Protector's ability is a strict if/otherwise effect with no "may": "If it's a unit, draw it. Otherwise, put it in your trash and give me +2 [S] this turn." You can't choose to send a revealed unit to the trash instead of drawing it, so there's no way to trade the unit for +2 Shield.

question: Can I move a unit with shuriken flip if the enemy unit is retreat?
answer:
Yes — the move still happens.

Shuriken Flip's damage and move are separate instructions. If the enemy unit "Retreats" (returns to hand) before the spell resolves, the damage part fizzles — the unit left the board, so the targeting relationship is severed — but the move part resolves normally as long as you have a friendly unit to move (that unit is the spell's other target; Rule 359.3.e.8; FAQ #11929). The enemy unit leaving doesn't stop your unit from moving to the destination you locked in when the spell was finalized.

question: Can you play Existential Dread on 2 units if you repeat it?
answer:
Yes. Existential Dread's [Repeat] [2] lets you execute its effect a second time, and each execution can target a different attacking enemy unit — so you can stun two units (or return one already-stunned unit to hand and stun another).

Both choices are locked in when the spell is finalized, so both targets must be attacking enemy units at that moment. Note that Repeat's cost can only be paid once per instance (Rule 820.1.c.3 / 746.1.c.3), so you get exactly two executions — not more. FAQ #11275 confirms the targeting for each Repeat execution is chosen independently.

question: If we use Rebuttal on an enemy Star-Crossed, can we choose a new target of that Star-Crossed on Ruin Runner?
answer:
It depends on whose Ruin Runner it is.

Your own Ruin Runner: Yes. When you take control of Star-Crossed via Rebuttal's [A], "friendly" and "enemy" re-anchor to you. Since you now control the spell, it's no longer an "enemy spell" to your Ruin Runner, so you can legally pick it as the mandatory "friendly unit" target (it would bounce to your hand).

Your opponent's Ruin Runner: No. Ruin Runner can't be chosen by enemy spells and abilities (Rule 758, 355.9.b; FAQ 8565), and Star-Crossed — now controlled by you — is an enemy spell relative to their Ruin Runner. You can't put it in the "enemy unit" slot, and it's not friendly to you, so it can't fill either slot.

One reminder: Star-Crossed's two targets are both mandatory. Even if you retarget onto your own Ruin Runner, you must still pick a legal enemy unit for the other slot (FAQ 12084).

question: Does the threshold of the gray reward you of on energy if you conquer without an opponent?
answer:
No. Threshold of the Gray only triggers "when combat starts here," and conquering an empty battlefield is a Non-Combat Showdown — no Combat is ever staged, so the trigger never fires and you get no energy.

Combat only starts when opposing players' units are present at the same battlefield (CR 458). Moving into an uncontested battlefield with no enemy units skips Combat entirely, so there's no attacker/defender trigger either. If your opponent later sends units in and an actual Combat Showdown begins, then the ability fires and both the attacker and defender each Add 1 energy — but a solo conquer gets nothing.

question: Can you react to Sunken Temple trigger if the person who conquers doesn't choose to pay 1 and draw 1?
answer:
No — if the conqueror declines the "may," there's nothing to react to. You only get a reaction window if they choose to pay and draw.

Sunken Temple's "you may pay [1] to draw 1" has the "you may" as the first part of its effect, so the controller's decision is made during finalization, before the trigger becomes a Finalized Chain Item (CR 383.3.a, 403.1). If they decline, the trigger is removed from the chain and considered to have not triggered (Rule 383.3.a.2) — it never hits the chain, so no player gets a chance to play Reactions.

If they do choose to pay and draw, the ability finalizes to the chain and then opens a normal Reaction window (CR 407.4). This is the key difference from something like Zaun Warrens, whose draw trigger is mandatory and always gives opponents a window to react.

question: Is Atakhan's "kill a defender" considered an ability for purposes of Ruin Runner?
answer:
Yes, but it doesn't help Ruin Runner — Atakhan's kill effect is an ability, yet it doesn't "choose" or target Ruin Runner, so the protection never applies.

Atakhan's "When I attack, the defender must kill one of their units here" is a triggered ability (Rule 383), and Ruin Runner's "I can't be chosen by enemy spells and abilities" (Rule 756–757) would block it if it targeted. But it doesn't — the defending player makes the choice of which unit to kill during resolution (Rule 355.10.e: "Each player kills a unit they control" does not target). So if Ruin Runner is the only unit there, its controller is forced to kill it (FAQ #9598, matching the Cull the Weak ruling, FAQ #8681).

question: What happens when you play Abandon on a spell that was played for its Flow cost?
answer:
It will be banished when it attempts to leave the chain.

“[T]hen banish it” in Flow’s text is short for “if it would leave the chain after becoming a finalized chain item, and leaving the chain wasn’t instructed by its own execution, banish it instead.” Abandon returns the countered card to hand after countering it, but for the purposes of Flow’s “then banish it”, this is also leaving the chain. No matter how it happens, as long as the Flow spell leaving the chain wasn’t instructed by the execution of the spell itself, it will be banished.

This also applies to effects like Kai’Sa, Evolutionary from Origins, or Fizz, Trickster from Spiritforged.

question: What is the difference between Iascylla and Azir, Sovereign’s uses of “this battlefield”?
answer:
Iascylla’s delayed trigger refers to the battlefield that she held. Azir, Sovereign’s attack trigger refers to the battlefield where he is located.

The difference between these two is that Iascylla has a delayed trigger that references implicit information from her trigger condition: the battlefield where she held. Azir, Sovereign’s attack trigger does not reference information from his trigger condition, which purely checks for the event of Azir gaining the attacker designation for the first time each combat. Without that information being checked from the trigger condition, the “this battlefield” in Azir, Sovereign’s attack trigger will be checked when the triggered ability resolves. If it resolves and he is not located at a battlefield, any instructions related to that battlefield will be ignored; otherwise, the battlefield he is currently located at will be used.

Comparatively, when a triggered ability refers to information from its trigger condition, that information is checked when the ability triggers and not on resolution. In the case of Iascylla, her delayed trigger is linked with her hold effect, so the information from the trigger condition of the hold effect can be shared with the delayed trigger.

In future sets, they’ve moved to use more precise templating and wording for abilities like Iascylla’s.

question: What happens when I play Moonfall choosing an enemy unit while I control an empowered Mel, Newly Awakened?
answer:
The chosen unit will be given -3 [M]. All other enemy units at the chosen battlefield will be given -2 [M].

Mel, Newly Awakened’s empowered ability is a replacement effect. It replaces the event of a spell or ability you control giving a unit it chooses -[M]. The event it replaces that with is the spell or ability giving an additional -1 [M].

Although Moonfall gives -[M] to multiple units, only one of them is chosen, and thus the only event that is eligible to be replaced is the chosen unit being given -2 [M]. It will be replaced with that unit being given -3 [M]. The events of the other units being given -[M] will not be affected by this replacement effect.

question: What about casting Stupefy while I have an empowered Mel, Newly Awakened?
answer:
The chosen unit will be given -2 [M], to a minimum of 1 [M]. If it was 2 [M], it will become 1 [M].

In the case of Stupefy, Mel, Newly Awakened replaces the event of Stupefy giving -1 [M] with it giving -2 [M] instead. However, a replacement effect that replaces an event modified by the game effect that generated that event will inherit any of those modifications. In this case, Stupefy modifies the “give -1 [M]” game action and thus event with “to a minimum of 1 [M].” The replaced event will inherit the same modification.

question: Speaking of Mel, can my opponent play Abandon on my spell while I control an empowered Mel, Newly Awakened? What happens?
answer:
They can play Abandon targeting your spell. On resolution, they will Predict, but nothing else will happen.

Mel, Newly Awakened says “your spells and abilities can’t be countered.” If the spell can’t be countered, Abandon will attempt to counter it and fail, and then it will replace the event of it being put in the Trash with it being returned to its owner’s hand. However, that event never occurred, so there is nothing for the replacement effect to replace. Thus, Abandon will resolve to no effect. The replacement effect only functions within the limit of the resolution of the ability (it’s not a delayed replacement effect that specifies a duration), so even if the spell resolves later, it will go to the Trash as normal.

question: How does it work if I cast Abandon while having an empowered Mel, Newly Awakened but they Rebuttal my spell?
answer: In the case of Rebuttal, gaining control of a spell is not the same thing as countering that spell. Effects that prevent spells being countered don’t prevent their controller from changing. If Rebuttal is played choosing your spell, and they pay [A] during resolution of Rebuttal, they will gain control of it. However, them not paying [A] does not mean the spell will be countered.

question: What new choices can I make when I play Rebuttal and pay [A]?
answer:
You can choose any number of targets or modes to make new choices for. The rest remain the same.

If you are remaking choices in this way, any choices you choose not to remake must be legal choices. You can’t choose to have some but not all choices be legal choices. Of course, you can always choose not to make new choices. In that case, any of the current choices will remain in their current state, whether that state is illegal or not.

If a spell has some rules or requirements about the choices made for it, those apply regardless of who controls that spell. For example, if a player plays a spell from face down, they must target game objects located at the battlefield the spell was played from unless the instructions of that spell indicate that a target must be chosen from some other location. Gaining control of such a spell doesn’t change this requirement when making new choices for the spell.

This section is expected to be revisited in a future rules update.

question: What happens if I choose to copy an empowered unit when I equip an unempowered unit with Shady Spectacles?
answer:
Being empowered is a status and is not copyable, thus the equipped unit will remain unempowered.

Shady Spectacles applies a copy effect to the equipped unit. Copy effects copy the copyable traits of the unit being copied, which include any traits it received from another copy effect that has already been applied. Empowered is a status, a temporary modification, and not part of the copyable traits of the card, so it will not be copied by Shady Spectacles. Whatever temporary modifications are applied to the unit as the copy effect is executed on that unit will be unaffected by the copy effect. If the unit has Might increases or decreases, a buff, the empowered status, Temporary, attacker, defender, etc those will remain in place.

question: What happens when my opponent’s Akshan, Mischievous steals my equipped Shady Spectacles? What happens if they want to copy Aphelios?
answer:
If it was attached to a unit, the equipped unit loses its copy effect. Akshan will then become a copy of a friendly unit of his controller’s choice. If he becomes a copy of Aphelios, his ability will not trigger.

As of the Vendetta rules update, effects like Shady Spectacles and Svellsongur are replacement effects that replace the event of the equipment being attached to a unit with that event plus whatever their effect specifies.

In the case of Svellsongur, the resulting series of events will be: Attach → Copy the equipped unit’s text to Svellsongur’s effect text for as long as Svellsongur is attached.

For Shady Spectacles, the resulting series of events will be: Attach → Choose a friendly unit and make the equipped unit a copy of that unit for as long as Shady Spectacles is attached.

These events are not simultaneous. The attach event executes first, and then whatever event is instructed by the replacement effect is executed. Thus, the answer in the Spiritforged FAQ is no longer true: if you attach Svellsongur to Aphelios, he will not trigger twice. Svellsongur doesn’t have the copied effect text when the attach event executes.

Similarly, if Akshan nabs Shady Spectacles from an opponent, it will attach and then make him a copy. If his controller chooses to make him a copy of Aphelios, it’s too late by that point for his new triggered ability to see the attachment event; it’s already been completed.

question: My Sand Soldier has Shady Spectacles equipped and is a copy of Azir, Ascendent. What happens if I activate the copied Azir’s activated ability before detaching the Shady Spectacles and then attach them to the same Sand Soldier as a copy of the same Azir, Ascendent? Can I use the activated ability again?
answer:
You can.

Each instance of the copied ability is a different ability. The game object remains the same throughout this whole process, so any temporary modifications will remain on the Sand Soldier as it transforms, but the copied rules text is an entirely new instance of the ability. It is the same idea as Svellsongur’s copy of an ability being “refreshed” if Svellsongur is detached and then reattached to the same unit.

question: What happens during combat damage assignment if my 4 [M] unit has both Ki Barrier and Lotus Trap played on it this turn and my opponent has a 4 [M] defender?
answer:
You can order the replacement effects on your unit. If Ki Barrier is first, your unit will take no damage and you will have 3 damage prevention remaining on your unit. If Lotus Trap is first, your unit will take 1 damage and will have no damage prevention remaining on your unit.

With the Vendetta rules update, replacement effects that apply to damage in combat are streamlined: any replacement effect that would apply to combat damage being dealt will apply instead to combat damage assignment. This was already the case for prevention effects like Ki Barrier or Counterstrike, to prevent several strange edge cases. Now, damage increasing replacement effects will also apply during damage assignment.

question: What happens when I discard a Patched Porobot with Hwei, Brooding Painter’s move trigger?
answer:
Two triggers will go on the chain, in the order of your choosing. One says “Give me +3 [M] this turn.” while the other says “Ready up to 2 runes.”

Hwei, Brooding Painter says “do the following based on the discarded card's type …” Unlike previous reflexive triggers that use a similar template (cf Twisted Fate, Gambler), Hwei doesn’t say “do one of the following …” As long as the card has the appropriate type, you will put the corresponding reflexive trigger on the chain. If somehow there existed a card that was a spell unit gear, you would put three reflexive triggers on the chain when you discard it to Hwei.

question: If my opponent plays two spells in succession, can I counter the first one with Crumbling Sands?
answer:
Yes.

Crumbling Sands uses the “finalize” meaning of play, because it checks whether cards have been “played” and isn’t a triggered ability. As long as an opponent (not even necessarily the one who played this spell) has chosen targets, paid costs, checked legality, and completed the process of finalizing another spell, even if that spell was countered, Crumbling Sands can counter a spell. That means it can counter the first spell played, as long as another spell was played by an opponent after that one.

question: When can I react to my opponent playing Fallen Feline to a battlefield? And how does naming a card work?
answer:
You can react to the play effect of Fallen Feline, before they’ve named a spell.

Fallen Feline’s play effect instructs its controller to name a spell. This occurs on resolution of the triggered ability. If Fallen Feline is played to a battlefield, as soon as the ability resolves, opponents cannot play spells with that name. Meaning spells by that name can not be put onto a chain. Any spells already on the chain when Fallen Feline’s ability resolves will be unaffected. However, by the time you know the chosen spell it’s too late to play that spell.

Naming a card or tag has new rules with the Vendetta rules update. When naming something in this way, the overarching rule is that you can’t name something that doesn’t exist in Riftbound. You can’t name the “Locke” tag, the “totem” type, nor a card named “Lingering Tentacles,” because none of those has been printed on cards or tokens in Riftbound.

However, you can name a card using information that uniquely identifies it. That information could be its name, but it could just as well be something like “the [3] spell with Flow that makes tentacles” or “the red Kai’Sa” or “Illaoi.” As long as there is no ambiguity as to what card is being named, a player can use whatever method is clear to their opponents and teammates. You can’t name a card by saying just “Kai’Sa” if there are two or more cards that could be identified in that way—you won’t have named a card if that’s all you say.

question: If I disempower a Kayle, Justified who has been empowered 3 times, does she lose all of her empowered statuses?
answer:
No. She will lose one of her empowered statuses.

For every Riftbound card other than Kayle, empowered is a binary status. They are either empowered or not. Kayle utilizes the golden rule “Card text supersedes rules text” to overcome this and be able to escape the normal bounds of what the empowered status means. On Kayle, empowered isn’t a binary status but a stacking status; she can have up to 3 empowered statuses. When Kayle is disempowered, the disempower action attempts to remove the empowered status. If she only has one empowered status, great, it’s gone. If she has more than one empowered status, the disempower action will remove one of the empowered statuses from Kayle.

question: Can I activate Kayle’s empower ability even if she’s already empowered?
answer:
Yes.

Kayle’s empower ability can be activated any number of times. If she has less than 3 empowered statuses, she will become empowered. If she has 3 empowered statuses, the ability can still be activated but nothing will happen when the ability resolves.

question: What happens if my opponent plays Flash on their Akali, Silent that’s currently in combat after I play Star-Crossed targeting her?
answer:
Akali will be unaffected by Star-Crossed as it resolves.

Akali, Silent is what the rules refer to as “untargetable” for enemy spells and abilities when she isn’t in combat; meaning she is not a legal target for them. Enemy spells and abilities being played when she’s untargetable can’t choose her. If she becomes untargetable after she’s already been chosen by an effect and retains it as that effect begins to resolve, it will “mistarget” her. She will be unaffected by any of the spell or ability’s instructions. If an instruction chooses only her, that instruction will be ignored.

question: I have a Ravenbloom Student on the board and I haven’t played any spells this turn. What happens when I play Rebuttal targeting my opponent’s Stupefy and pay [A] on resolution? After everything resolves, how much will Battering Ram cost? Will my opponent’s Legion abilities be active?
answer:
Ravenbloom Student will trigger twice, Battering Ram will cost [4], and your opponent’s Legion abilities will be active.

Ravenbloom Student’s triggered ability checks whether a spell that you control resolves. You gained control of the Stupefy, and it resolved, so you will have triggered Ravenbloom Student’s ability. Battering Ram and Legion, on the other hand, check whether cards were finalized. Although you gained control of Stupefy, you did not finalize it; you got it after it was already finalized by your opponent. Thus, your opponent’s Legion abilities will be active, and Battering Ram will only receive a [1] Energy discount.

question: What happens when I conquer with Swain, Visionary, if I’ve only played a Patched Porobot and Stupefy this turn?
answer:
You will score 2 points total. 1 from conquering, 1 from Swain.

Swain only checks whether you’ve played a non-token unit, a non-token gear, and a spell. Checks like that do not care whether they were satisfied by multiple cards or a single card relevant to the trigger conditions.

question: What happens when my opponent plays Switcheroo on their 2 [M] unit and my empowered Gangplank, Naval?
answer:
Gangplank, Naval will replace his Might being lowered with him being given +3 [M] this turn.

Swap calculates the difference in Might and generates two effects: an increase, and a decrease. When a swap effect is applied to two units’ Mights, it gives those units +[M] and -[M] respective to who has the higher Might.

Under the hood, Gangplank’s replacement effect sees the event of him being given -[M] and replaces it with him being given +3 [M] this turn instead. The event of the other unit being given +[M] is unaffected by Gangplank’s replacement effect. By the time we apply the replacement effect, the difference between the two units has been calculated. In the example with the 2 [M] unit, the final Mights of the two units will be 2 [M] → 6 [M], and 6 [M] → 9 [M].

The way this works is not immediately obvious based on how the swap game action rules are written. This is expected to be clarified in a future rules update.

Note that this logic also applies to Mel, Newly Awakened and Switcheroo.

question: What happens when my empowered Gangplank, Naval is moved by my opponent’s Blast Cone’s play effect and they exhaust Blast Cone to stun Gangplank? Will he be stunned? What happens if I then play Back Off choosing my Gangplank? Will he get +3 [M] this turn?
answer:
Blast Cone will stun Gangplank. If you play Back Off choosing your stunned Gangplank, he will not receive +3 [M] this turn.

Blast Cone’s triggered ability that stuns units doesn’t choose them, so Gangplank’s replacement effect can’t apply to that event. Back Off played on a stunned Gangplank does not actually perform the stun game action, because Gangplank is already stunned. It’s legal to play Back Off, but the instruction will be negated. In order for Gangplank’s replacement effect to replace an event of him being stunned, the stun game action must actually be performed. Similarly, if an effect that said “Friendly units can’t be stunned” were active with a friendly empowered Gangplank, Naval on the board, a stun effect that is played choosing Gangplank wouldn’t generate an event that Gangplank could replace, because no stun game action is performed.

question: What happens if I play Stupefy on my 1 [M] empowered Gangplank, Naval? Will he get +3 [M] this turn?
answer:
He will not.

In order for his replacement effect to apply, the event of him being given -[M] must occur. In the case of Stupefy played on a 1 [M] unit, no -[M] is given; it is snapshot to -0 [M]. Thus, there is no suitable event for Gangplank’s replacement effect to replace.

question: What happens when my opponent plays Hidden Blade targeting my Akali, Deadly Weapon in reaction to her move trigger? Will it still deal damage to the chosen unit?
answer:
It will.

Akali is another case where her ability refers to information implicit to its own trigger condition, similar to Iascylla. Akali’s “battlefield I moved to or from” doesn’t require her to be on the board in order for us to be able to identify it, nor does it reference information about her current state. Even if she leaves the board, that information was checked when her ability triggered, and it is still available to us on resolution.

question: Can I activate an empowered Heimerdinger, Inventor to ready 2 gear if my Jayce, Defender of Tomorrow legend isn’t empowered? What about if my Heimerdinger isn’t empowered?
answer:
You can activate Heimerdinger’s ability if he is empowered, regardless of the empowered status of Jayce, Defender of Tomorrow.

There are two important details relating to dependent keywords:

A dependent keyword (the kind of ability that [Level][>] or [Empowered][>] are when they appear with the arrow) includes the whole of the ability, including the dependent ability. They’re all one object, so to speak.

A dependent keyword’s dependent ability still exists and can be referenced while it is inactive—that is, if its condition isn’t met. In this case, the condition is that the source of the ability is empowered.

Heimerdinger gains all activated abilities that have the [E] symbol in their cost, and he gains the entire ability, restrictions, costs, dependent keywords and all. In effect, Defender of Tomorrow’s ability that Heimerdinger is gaining is the whole line that says: [Empowered][>] [1], [E]: Ready 2 gear.

Heimerdinger can gain this ability even if Defender of Tomorrow isn’t empowered because of that second point.

The key rule is 727.1.b.1.: The Dependent Ability is present on the card for the sake of reference or evaluation until the Condition is met. This means that the ability isn’t active and its text isn’t being processed yet, but other effects can reference or evaluate its text before the condition is met. Heimerdinger, Inventor is exactly one such effect.

question: What card does Astral Heron’s triggered ability discount?
answer:
It discounts the next card played (added to the chain and queued for finalization) this turn after the ability resolves.

Astral Heron has received an erratum to update its wording: “When you play your first card each turn, if I'm at a battlefield, the next card you play this turn costs [2][A][A] less.”

question: What happens when I play Temporal Breach targeting my Elder Dragon in base and pay [A][A] for Dragon Roost while playing Elder Dragon? Will it be played to base or to Dragon Roost?
answer:
You can choose which of those two locations you want to play it to.

In general, there are not many cases with competing instructions: one effect that tells you to play a unit to one location, and one that tells you to play it to another. When they arise with contradictory requirements, the precedent from other areas of the rules is that the player chooses one of those requirements and ignores all others.

Note that this only applies to mandatory positive requirements, ones that specify a location or method without also preventing the action from being performed to other locations or with other methods and that aren’t optional. For example, an effect like Perched Grimwyrm’s passive ability is a restriction on playing that unit to any location other than a battlefield you’ve conquered this turn. Rockfall Path’s passive ability is a restriction on playing units to Rockfall Path. If you’ve conquered only Rockfall Path this turn, you can’t play Perched Grimwyrm at all, because those two restrictions are contradictory.

In this case, the contradictory requirements don’t directly prohibit the playing of these units to other locations, so we can choose one of the contradictory requirements and ignore the rest.

question: What happens when I play Perched Grimwyrm while I haven’t conquered Dragon Roost this turn? Can I pay [A][A] and play it to Dragon Roost? What if I’ve conquered another battlefield this turn?
answer:
You cannot.

In Riftbound, “can’t” beats “can.” Perched Grimwyrm’s effect is a “can’t,” as in it can’t be played to any location but to a battlefield you’ve conquered this turn. Dragon Roost’s ability tries to give the Grimwyrm permission to be played to the Roost, but that can’t overcome Perched Grimwyrm’s own restriction. If you have no ability to play Perched Grimwyrm to Dragon Roost after paying for it, you will not be able to finalize Perched Grimwyrm at all. The actions taken as part of playing Perched Grimwyrm will be undone and it will be returned to the zone it was played from.

This is true even if you’ve conquered another battlefield this turn. If you have the ability, you can play Perched Grimwyrm to that battlefield without paying the additional cost of Dragon Roost, but you can’t play it to Dragon Roost itself unless you’ve conquered it.

Baron Nashor doesn’t work this way. He enters at the Baron Pit regardless of effects preventing him from being played to battlefields, because Baron Nashor’s passive ability generates a delayed replacement effect (“I enter there”) that replaces the event of him entering to any other location with him entering to the Baron Pit. That replacement effect gets around effects like Mageseeker Warden. Dragon Roost is not written as a replacement effect. It tells you where to play the dragon you’ve paid the additional cost for, but it doesn’t specify how that dragon enters the board. Therefore it is a permission on play location, but not a replacement effect.

question: Can I disempower my Ambessa, Matriarch of War with Profiteer to empower my Kayle? Do I control my own legend?
answer:
Yes, you can disempower Ambessa, Matriarch of War with Profiteer. And yes, you control your own legend.

We don’t typically consider the possibility that any player controls a legend, because control of legends cannot change, but you do indeed control your own legend.

question: What happens if I play Dragon Form on a unit that has -1 [M] from Stupefy applied to it? Will my Fiora, Grand Duelist trigger? Is there a moment where my unit becomes 5 [M] before the -1 [M] from Stupefy brings it down to 4 [M]?
answer:
She will not trigger.

Although Dragon Form sets the base Might of a unit to 5 [M], it does so via layers. Layers are evaluated when the effect is applied and their evaluation includes all existing applied layer alterations. We process layers in order, starting from the Trait-Altering layer (where this base Might setting effect is applied), proceeding to the Ability-Altering layer (not part of this example), and proceeding to the Arithmetic layer (where Stupefy’s -1 [M] is applied), but this process happens instantaneously; there is no window while evaluating layers for the unit to see itself become 5 [M] and then go down to 4 [M]. As soon as the effect of Dragon Form is applied, the unit is 4 [M].

As a side note, Might is one of the traits that is managed in the Trait-Altering layer, and it is one of the copyable traits that copy effects can replace or add to.

question: What happens when I play Hostile Takeover gaining control of my opponent’s ready unit, move it to base, and then play Temporal Breach choosing it? Where will the unit go?
answer:
The unit will remain in Banishment.

Units cannot be played to a base of a player other than their own controller under any circumstances. Because the owner of the unit is the one being instructed to play the unit, and the location they are being instructed to play it to is a base other than their own, it isn’t possible to play the unit. During the check legality step of finalization, the unit will be returned to banishment from the chain and all actions taken will be undone.

question: My 11 Might Renekton, Brute is disempowered by my own Profiteer. What happens when my opponent plays Stupefy choosing him? Will his ability trigger? What happens if instead I activated his ability?
answer:
Renekton’s ability will not trigger in either scenario.

In order to “become 10 or more,” his Might would have to have previously been less than 10. “10 or more” is a state, and Renekton’s triggered ability checks for the event of him achieving that state. If he maintains that state, regardless of how his Might changes, he will not “become” that state.

question: What happens when I play Icathian Rain choosing a Recruit at Heisho, Shell of the World once and Irelia, Fervent in base five times? How many times do I pay for deflect?
answer:
You will not pay for deflect.

While your spell or ability chooses a unit at Heisho, Shell of the World, you ignore deflect while paying for the spell. Ignore, in this context, means you treat deflect on the specified units as being inactive, like it’s turned off temporarily. In the case of Heisho, it doesn’t specify any units whose deflect to ignore, so you ignore all instances of deflect on units.

This only applies to the specified spell or ability. You can’t play a spell or ability choosing a unit at Heisho, and then play another one choosing a unit at another location and not at Heisho and still ignore deflect. Only while at least one target of the spell or ability is a unit located at Heisho do you ignore deflect while paying costs for that spell or ability.

question: What happens when I play Hextech Ray on an Elder Dragon while Imperial Decree’s delayed trigger is active and I have an Immortal Phoenix in the Trash? Can I play Immortal Phoenix from the Trash?
answer:
You can.

Per the current rules, there is nothing that would stop Imperial Decree’s delayed trigger from triggering Immortal Phoenix. It is a triggered ability generated by a spell; it is attributed a kill action, and thus the spell that generated it will also be attributed the same kill action. The owner of Imperial Decree is the controller of the delayed triggered ability; the player responsible for the kill action is the one who controls the ability; and that same player is the owner of Immortal Phoenix in the Trash. Thus all three conditions for Immortal Phoenix triggering are complete, and it will trigger.

question: If I play Ride the Wind targeting my unit at Vilemaw’s Lair and attempt to move them to base, what happens?
answer:
They will be readied.

This is a rules quirk that players and judges identified as a result of a small additional rule added in the Vendetta rules update. This isn’t an actual change to how this has been interpreted and ruled on previously — it’s smoothing out a bug in how broadly “ignored” instructions were defined.

An ignored instruction is one that wasn’t performed as part of the execution of a spell or ability’s instructions because it mistargeted (i.e. because the targeted object wasn’t a legal target on resolution). For example, you play Hidden Blade choosing an enemy unit and they play Star-Crossed in reaction, returning their unit to hand — when Hidden Blade resolves, the unit isn’t on the board, so we ignore the “Its controller draws 2.” instruction. Alternatively, if Hidden Blade is given the Repeat keyword by the Academy and both executions target the same unit, this is why the unit’s controller doesn’t draw 4 cards.

An instruction is not ignored if an ability, effect, or circumstance of the game prevents it from occurring. That could be a replacement effect, an ability like Vilemaw’s Lair that says “Units can’t move from here to base,” a game action like Buff or Ready on a unit that already has the appropriate state, or a unit/gear/spell no longer being in an appropriate zone as long as the instruction doesn’t target those objects. In those cases the instruction isn’t ignored, but instead negated. A negated instruction has its effects skipped, replaced, or prevented.
