question: What is the difference between "finalize" and "resolution"?
answer:
Finalizing is completing the steps of playing an item (choices, costs, legality) and turning it from Pending into a Finalized Chain Item; resolution is the later step where the item's actual game effects execute.

Finalize is Step 1 of FEPR (Rule 337): the controller makes choices, determines and pays costs, and checks legality, then the item stops being Pending (Rule 359.1). No game effects happen here, and finalizing doesn't pass priority (Rule 337.1.a).

Resolve is Step 4 (Rule 340): the newest Finalized Chain Item executes its rules text in its entirety (Rule 340.1). For Units and Gear, finalize and resolve happen back-to-back — they leave the Chain and enter the board immediately (Rules 337.2, 359.2). Spells instead linger on the Chain after finalizing so opponents get a Reaction window, and only resolve later (Rule 359.3.c–d).

The practical difference: finalize = "is this card valid, paid for, and locked in?", resolve = "what does it actually do?"

question: What is restoring game state and deck state
answer:
Restoring game state and deck state are judge remedies for fixing errors — not a single mechanic.

Restoring the game state means rewinding the game to the state before an error occurred. Each action since the error is reversed in reverse order (TR 701.5). A simple rewind (only the most recent action) can be done by any judge; anything bigger requires the head judge or designated appeals judges. Any card whose identity became known during the error (e.g. a wrongly drawn card) is replaced with a random card so no information advantage survives, and any known cards in a deck are shuffled back into the randomized portion.

Restoring the deck state means making a deck's contents legal again after a setup/presentation error (TR 703.4, Deck Presentation Error) — undoing sideboarding for game one, pulling a Champion that was shuffled into the deck back to the Champion Zone, or fixing an illegal deck size. The judge moves cards back to their correct zones (including swapping sideboard cards out of a hand for random main-deck cards) and shuffles the randomized portion. If the deck can't be restored, the penalty escalates toward a Game Loss. Decks must also be returned to their registered state before the first game of the next match (TR 403.8).

question: In high opl when judge can interrupt a game?
answer:
A judge can interrupt a match at high OPL only in three situations: they believe a rules or policy violation has occurred, a player requests assistance, or they observe Unsporting Conduct (Rule 701.1.d).

Otherwise, judges are told not to intervene — they should not stop errors from occurring, only deal with errors that have already happened (Rule 701.1.c). Players can also pause at any time to flag a floor judge (Rule 412.1), and deck checks at high OPL are an allowed interruption (Rule 411). One important limit: a judge who discovers a previous ruling was wrong should wait until the current match is over rather than interrupt the ongoing game (FAQ 5409).

Interrupting doesn't change the remedy, though. A forgotten trigger never goes on the Chain (TR 506.4). answer:
The opponent is right — the judge should not shuffle the whole hand back and redraw, because that hands the erroring player a free mulligan at high OPL. The correct remedy is a minimal Deck Presentation Error fix (TR 703.4), not a rewind (TR 701.5).

The battlefield card is removed from wherever it is — out of the hand if it was drawn, or out of the deck — and placed in the Battlefield Zone. If it was in the hand, that one card is replaced by a random card from the randomized portion of the deck, and only that portion is shuffled (TR 701.4.a). The rest of the hand is untouched, so no redraw advantage exists. This mirrors the champion-in-deck ruling (FAQ #4469), which fixes the zone error without rewinding the draw.

Penalty at high OPL: Warning if the erroring player self-reports; Game Loss if the opponent or a spectator caught it after opening hands were drawn (TR 703.4.c.3). There is no downgrade for forgotten setup cards, so it does not apply to battlefields.

question: What happens if an attacker and surprise defender is a tie but both stunned
answer:
The combat is a tie and the attacker is recalled — the defender keeps the battlefield and conquers it.

Since both sides are stunned, neither contributes Might to combat damage (CR 424.1.b), so no damage is dealt and both units survive — a stunned unit still needs its full Might in damage to be killed (CR 424.1.c). At Combat Cleanup, all units heal and the attackers are recalled because defenders are still present (466.1.a.2). With only the defender's stunned unit left, the defender establishes control and scores a Conquer if they haven't already scored that battlefield this turn (466.5, 469.1).

Stun doesn't change this: a stunned unit still holds a battlefield and conquers. The defender's unit stays stunned until end-of-turn cleanup (423.1.a.2), and the combat result is "No Result," so nothing like "when I win a combat" triggers for either player.

question: when sett brawler enters play as a 4 might unit, and gets might reduced (by stupefy for example) before his buff. at the end of turn, when stupefy expires, does sett player trigger fiora legend ability
answer:
Yes. When Stupefy expires at end of turn, Sett's Might goes from 4 to 5 (base 4 + his permanent buff), and that transition from below 5 to 5+ is exactly when a unit "becomes Mighty" (Rule 709), triggering Fiora, Grand Duelist.

This is the same interaction as any temporary -Might effect wearing off: the "this turn" effect is removed during expiration, Sett's Might re-evaluates to 5, and Fiora's trigger fires and goes on the chain. Players can even respond to that trigger before the next phase — effects played in response just won't be cleansed until the next end of turn (FAQ #742, #358).

Note: Sett's play buff is a permanent counter and doesn't expire, so it's Stupefy dropping — not the buff running out — that makes him go 4 → 5 at cleanup.

question: Player B forgot to track point Player A has a note on points how the game goes?
answer:
The game proceeds with the point corrected. If Player A's note lets the judge determine the correct score, and no more than a full round cycle has passed since the miss, the appropriate player's score is incremented to the correct total (Tournament Rule 702.3.b.1). Notes are legitimate evidence for that determination.

Once a full round cycle has passed (i.e., the turn player's next turn rolls around), the point can no longer be fixed and play just continues at the tracked score (702.3.b.2). Either way, a score discrepancy must be announced to all players immediately when noticed — per TR 415.3.b, if it can't be resolved easily, call a judge. Note this only covers Conquer/Hold points; points from card triggers like Ahri, Alluring are missed triggers and aren't given back (702.3.a).

question: If a might 4 unit with master yi legend are defending a might 2. And get switcheeroo, does the +2 from defending alone still applied last?
answer:
Yes — but the +2 is already baked into the swap, so your defender ends at 2 Might, not 4, and the attacker jumps to 6.

Switcheroo snapshots each unit's current Might at resolution — your defender is 6 (4 base + 2 from Master Yi) and the attacker is 2 — then applies a fixed −4 to the defender and +4 to the attacker (CR 434.1.b). Master Yi's +2 is a continuous passive that keeps applying while the unit defends alone, but since it was part of the value Switcheroo swapped, you don't get it added on top again: 4 + 2 − 4 = 2 for the defender, 2 + 4 = 6 for the attacker (RiftJudge FAQ #341 — passives stay on their original units and don't re-stack over the swap).

question: In low opl if an opponent doesn't come, does 10 minutes rule apply?
answer:
Yes — the 10-minute clock applies at every OPL, including low OPL (TR 703.8).

The only OPL difference is the middle tier: arriving within 10 minutes of round start is a Warning + time extension at low OPL (upgraded to Game Loss only at high OPL). Past 10 minutes it's a Match Loss at any level, and if the opponent never shows, they get a Match Loss and are dropped from the tournament unless they report to a judge before the next match begins (TR 703.8.c–d).

question: If a mech unit with rumble scrapper gets coppied does the rumble scrapper effect adds another +2
answer:
Yes — if the copied unit is Rumble, Scrapper himself. Copy effects copy his rules text and tags (Rule 479.1.b.1), so a Reflection/Mirror Image copy is a second Rumble with his own static "Your Mechs have +1 [M] (including me)" ability, and two separate sources stack: your Mechs get +2 total, and each Rumble gets +1 from both abilities (6 Might).

If instead you meant copying some other Mech while Rumble is on the board: no +2. The copy comes in at its printed Might — copy effects don't include bonuses granted by other cards — and then Rumble's effect applies exactly once, giving it the same +1 every other Mech gets.

question: Can you give me a riftbound layer?
answer:
There are three layers, and they loop until every applicable effect has been applied once and nothing changes (CR 478).

Trait-Altering (CR 479.2) — changes to Name, Supertype, Type, Tags, Controller, Cost, Domain. Copy effects and "Might becomes X" settings happen here.

Ability-Altering (CR 479.3) — grants/removes keywords, passive abilities, or rules text (e.g. "Other friendly units have Vision"), plus attached-card effect text.

Arithmetic (CR 479.4) — numeric +/- to Might, Energy Cost, Power Cost. Increases apply first, then decreases; non-passive limitations are snapshot at application.

Because layers loop, an effect applied in layer 3 can enable a layer-1/2 effect that wasn't applicable before — e.g. Fiora, Victorious: her Might buff bumps her past Mighty in the Arithmetic layer, then the sequence re-runs and she gains Deflect, Ganking, and Shield (CR 478.3, example). Within a single layer, dependencies apply first, otherwise timestamp order (FAQ 5401).

question: Can you show me riftbound layering
answer:
Sure — Riftbound's layers (CR 475–482) are the ordered system that decides how game effects modify traits, keywords, and numbers. There are three, applied top to bottom:

Trait-Altering (477.1) — changes to name, supertype, type, tags, controller, cost, domain, and Might-setting effects like "Might becomes 4." Copy effects (e.g. becoming a copy of another card) also apply here.

Ability-Altering (477.2) — granting/removing keywords and passive abilities, appending or removing rules text (including text from attached Gear).

Arithmetic (477.3) — the +/− math on Might and costs. Increases apply before decreases, and non-passive limits are "snapshotted" at the moment they apply.

After one pass through all three, the layers loop: re-evaluate and apply any effect that newly became applicable (476). Each effect only applies once per evaluation, and once a full pass changes nothing, you're done. That's what makes things like Fiora, Victorious work — her buff raises Might in Arithmetic, the loop re-checks Layer 2, and now "While I'm Mighty" grants her Deflect, Ganking, and Shield (476.3).

When multiple effects hit the same object in the same layer: check dependency first (if one effect's application changes the other's outcome, apply the depended-on one first — 478–479), otherwise fall back to timestamp order, earliest first (480).

question: Dose soraka save units if she also dies herself at the same time
answer:
Yes. Under the current rules (v1.4), Soraka can save other units at her location that die simultaneously with her.

Rule 370.4 explicitly states that a game object can apply its replacement effects to qualifying events that occur simultaneously with it leaving the board — with Soraka, Wanderer as the named example. Earlier community/FAQ answers said "no" based on ambiguity in older rules, but that gap was closed by the replacement-effects clarification (Core Rules 2026-07-16). The main limit: Soraka's save can only apply to units at her location ("here"), and her effect can only be applied in one sequence per batch of simultaneous events (Rule 373.2).

question: How does snapshot work in riftbound
answer:
Snapshotting is Riftbound's rule that a non-passive effect's numbers are locked in ("remembered") at the moment the effect applies — they don't re-evaluate later.

CR 479.4.b: when an arithmetic effect that isn't a passive ability has a limitation (like a min/max or a target's current Might), that limitation is snapshotted at the time of application and kept at that level for the whole duration. Example: "-4 Might to a min of 1" on a 2-Might unit becomes a permanent (for the duration) -1, not a fluctuating -4 that re-checks.

Two key corollaries:

Passive abilities do NOT snapshot — they re-evaluate continuously ("Units you control here have 5 Might" stays live).

Spells/abilities DO snapshot at resolution — effects only apply to what's present when the spell resolves, and numbers are fixed then; things entering play later during the duration are not affected (FAQ #7876). This also interacts with layers: increases apply before decreases (477.3.e), each with their own snapshotted limitations.

question: Can you cast repulse without a spell target, just with a creature target? Just to get a ''when you play a spell effect''?
answer:
No. Repulse requires both targets — a friendly unit at a battlefield and an enemy spell or ability on the chain that chooses that unit and no other friendly unit. The counter instruction is mandatory, not optional ("Counter..." with no "up to" or "may").

Without a qualifying enemy spell/ability on the chain, Repulse fails the check at finalization that the card made appropriate choices, since its targets aren't legal (Rule 358.1), and can't be played at all — even just to trigger "when you play a spell" effects. This matches the ruling for Riposte ("Choose a friendly unit and a spell"): every choice in the list is a mandatory target, and all must be legal before the spell can go on the chain.

question: If you play astral heron and its ability goes on the chain and the opponent plays star cross on it does it resolve
answer:
Yes — once Astral Heron's trigger is on the chain, bouncing it with Star-Crossed doesn't stop the ability from resolving.

The "if I'm at a battlefield" check happens at the moment the trigger fires, not when it resolves (Rule 383.2.c). Since the trigger fires after your first card has resolved, Heron was on the board at a battlefield at that moment, so the discount is created. Star-Crossed resolves first and returns Heron to your hand, but the ability is already a Finalized Chain Item and resolves independently of its source — your next card this turn still costs [2][A][A] less (FAQ #11829, #11792).

One caveat: if Heron itself is your first card and you played it to Base, it's not "at a battlefield" when the trigger fires, so the ability won't fire at all.

question: Can Dianas energy be used against an opponent who is in an open showdown (for example to play gust when they attempt to conquer an empty battlefield?)
answer:
Yes — you can play Gust during an opponent's conquest attempt, and Diana's trigger works there too, but Diana doesn't produce energy herself.

First, a clarification: Diana, Lunari's ability is a trigger ("When a showdown begins here, you may pay [1] to Predict, then reveal… draw it if it's a spell") — it spends [1], it doesn't generate it. That trigger does fire when the opponent starts a non-combat showdown at her battlefield on their turn (FAQ #9373), and you can pay the [1] then.

The energy comes from your runes, not Diana. Your rune pool empties at the start of each player's Main Phase and end of each turn (Rule 167), so by the opponent's showdown it's empty — but basic runes have Reaction Add abilities ([E]: [Reaction] — Add [1], Rule 164.2.a), and Reaction works on any player's turn in any state, so you just exhaust ready runes to pay Diana's cost and/or Gust's [1] cost.

Gust is a Reaction spell, so it's legally timed during the Showdown Open state of that conquest attempt (Rule 813). If it bounces the moved unit (3 Might or less), the showdown still continues until all players pass Focus, but with no unit remaining the attacker can't establish control when it closes — so no Conquer happens (Rule 348.2.a).

question: Can I use the 1 energy produced by Diana, Scorn of the Moon during my opponents open showdown. For example to use it to play "Gust" against their unit before it conquers?

Yes — that energy is spendable during your opponent's showdown, and you can use it to play Gust before the conquer resolves.

Scorn of the Moon's restriction is only "Spend this Energy only during showdowns" — it doesn't care whose showdown or whose turn it is. Activate Scorn of the Moon at Reaction speed (its ability has [Reaction], and Add abilities can't be reacted to), which puts 1 energy in your Rune Pool. Gust is a [Reaction] spell, so it's legally timed in a Showdown Open state when you have Focus (and even in the Showdown Closed state while a chain exists). You can also activate Scorn of the Moon directly during step 4 (pay costs) of playing Gust (Rule 357.1.a).

Two timing notes: you must play Gust while the showdown is still open — if both players pass and the showdown closes, the opponent establishes Control/Conquers (Rule 348.2) and there's no reaction window to stop it after the fact. And if the showdown ends with the energy unspent, it can't be used outside a showdown and will be lost when the Rune Pool empties (Rule 167).

question: Layering in riftbound explanation
answer:
Layers (CR 475–482) are the ordered system that decides how effects modify a card's traits, keywords, and numbers — and they loop until nothing changes.

There are three layers, applied top to bottom:

Trait-Altering (477.1) — name, supertype, type, tags, controller, cost, domain, copy effects, and Might setting ("Might becomes 4").

Ability-Altering (477.2) — granting/removing keywords and passive abilities, appending/removing rules text (including attached Gear text).

Arithmetic (477.3) — the +/− math on Might, Energy Cost, and Power Cost. Increases apply before decreases, and non-passive limitations are "snapshotted" when they apply.

The twist: after one pass, the sequence re-runs (CR 478). An effect applied in the Arithmetic layer can enable a layer-2 effect that wasn't applicable before. Example: Fiora, Victorious (4 Might, "While I'm Mighty, I have Deflect, Ganking, and Shield") gets a buff → Arithmetic bumps her to 5 → the loop re-checks layer 2 → she now gains the three keywords. When the buff leaves, she drops straight back to 4 with no keywords.

Within a single layer, check dependency first (if one effect changes another's outcome, apply the depended-on one first — CR 480–481); if no dependency, fall back to timestamp order, earliest first (CR 482).

question: Does static ability reevaluate like your mech get +2 after being switcheroo
answer:
No — a static/passive Might bonus doesn't reapply on top of the swap; it was already part of the numbers Switcheroo swapped.

Example: Rumble, Scrapper's "+1 Might to your Mechs" keeps applying before, during, and after the swap. A 3-Might Mech sitting at 4 thanks to Rumble that swaps with a 6-Might unit gets a +2 modifier, so it ends at exactly 6 (3 + 1 + 2) — no extra +1 added afterwards. The swap modifier is calculated against the current Might including passives (CR 434.1), so the passive doesn't stack a second time.

The only case where the passive changes the result is if its source changes after the swap resolves (e.g., Rumble leaves the board or enters later) — then the layers re-evaluate and the fixed swap modifier stays, shifting the total accordingly (Rule 479.4).

question: Definition of each layering in riftbound in simple definiton
answer:
Layers are the ordered system that decides how effects modify a card's traits, abilities, and numbers (CR 476–482). They apply top to bottom, then loop until nothing changes.

Trait-Altering — changes what a card is: Name, Supertype, Type, Tags, Controller, Cost, Domain, copy effects, and "Might becomes X" settings.

Ability-Altering — changes what a card does: granting/removing keywords, passive abilities, or rules text (including attached Gear text).

Arithmetic — the plain +/− math: Might, Energy Cost, Power Cost. Increases apply before decreases.

Because layers loop, a Layer 3 buff can enable a Layer 2 keyword — e.g., Fiora, Victorious gains her keywords only after her Might buff pushes her past "Mighty" (CR 478.4). Within one layer, dependent effects resolve dependencies first; otherwise timestamp order (CR 480–482).

question: Does a +2 from rumble scrapper is arithmetic or trait altering?
answer:
Arithmetic, not trait-altering — and to be precise, Rumble, Scrapper grants +1 Might to your Mechs, not +2.

CR 479.4.a puts increases and decreases to Might in the Arithmetic layer, which is where "+1 Might" from Rumble's passive applies. The Trait-Altering layer (477.1) handles things like Name, Type, Tags, and assignment of Might (e.g. "Might becomes 4"), not numeric bonuses. Since Rumble's bonus is an increase from a passive ability, it also never snapshots — it re-evaluates continuously per CR 479.4.b.

Practically, this matters for order of operations: because it's arithmetic, the +1 applies on top of any setting effect, and two sources of +1 (like a copy of Rumble) both stack.

answer:

Nothing is "locked" — if a unit later leaves the camp, it just loses the +1 on top of the swap modifier (CR 434.1; layers loop until stable, CR 478). FAQ #11637 confirms this is the intended handling.

question: If 2 arithmatic layer happens in same time
answer:
Both effects still apply — and each applies only once. Order in the Arithmetic layer is decided in three steps: first Dependency (CR 480) — if one effect changes what the other does, the independent one applies first and the dependent one second (e.g. the example in CR 481). If there's no dependency, timestamp order (CR 482) applies, earliest effect first.

For a true same-timestamp tie, Riftbound's rules don't define a tiebreaker (the FAQ flags this as a known gap), but two sub-rules still do work: within the Arithmetic layer, increases are applied before decreases (CR 479.4.e), and in practice, if both effects are plain +X/−X bonuses, the order doesn't change the final number — order only matters when a min/max limitation or a dependency is involved.

question: after conquering a battlefield can i pay 1 to put irelia trigger conquer ability on the stack even when the legen is already ready?

The trigger condition ("when you conquer") has no requirement that she be exhausted, and the cost is just 1 energy — not "exhaust her." Per CR 416.1.c, being told to ready an already-ready unit is a legal instruction that simply does nothing. So you can finalize the trigger, pay the 1, and on resolution "ready me" is a no-op.

One practical note: nothing about the legend actually becomes ready, so any "when I'm readied" or "when you ready" effects won't fire — you're just spending 1 energy (CR 383.3.b.1, 416.1.c).

If you decline to pay the [A], Rebuttal just counters the spell instead, and a countered spell is never considered played (CR 426.1.b) — so only Rebuttal's own trigger fires, for +1 once.

question: Does layer always appear in every chain
answer:
No — layers and the Chain are separate game systems, and one does not imply the other.

Layers (CR 475–482) are the evaluation framework for how Game Effects alter traits, abilities, and numbers on objects. They run as part of continuous characteristic evaluation — whenever an effect needs to be applied, a chain or not. The Chain (CR 327–331) is a temporary zone that only exists while a card is being played or an ability activated.

So a Chain can form and resolve with zero layer activity (e.g., drawing a card, dealing damage), and layers get applied constantly outside any Chain (passive auras, buff counters, Combat Cleanup). The two only interact in that a resolved effect may cause a layer evaluation — but layers are not a Chain item, step, or event.

question: If player A play a rengar with ambush ability and player B play tideturner making vex move to battlefield does the rengar stun?
answer:
Yes — Rengar gets stunned, assuming Vex was at a battlefield when Rengar entered.

Vex's ability is "When an opponent plays a unit while I'm at a battlefield, [Stun] it" — the only thing that matters is Vex's location at the instant the unit is played (Rule 383.2.c). When you play Rengar via Ambush in reaction to Tideturner, Tideturner's swap trigger hasn't resolved yet, so Vex is still where she started; if that's a battlefield, her trigger fires, stuns Rengar, and locks him from moving this turn. Ambush doesn't bypass it, and it doesn't matter that Rengar was played elsewhere (FAQs #10318, #11632).

The one exception: if Vex was sitting at a Base when Rengar entered, the trigger doesn't fire — and Vex arriving later via the swap won't retroactively stun him.

question: can i use retreat to target a non friendly unit just to cast the spell and burn it? if i just want to get a card played and dont care if it fizzles. any ways?
answer:
No — you can't. Retreat's "friendly unit" restriction means enemy units are illegal targets (Rule 355.9.b), and you can't put a spell on the chain without legal targets (355.8). If your only units are gone, Retreat simply can't be played at all — so there's no way to burn it just for a "when you play a spell" trigger.

The closest edge case: if you do have a friendly unit, you must target it, and it won't fizzle — the bounce resolves normally ("silver rule": you do as much as possible, FAQ #7360). The spell only whiffs if your target gets removed before it resolves (e.g., something else bounces or kills it in reaction). In that case it still counts as "played" for triggers like Red Darius (FAQ #3712), but you can't engineer that on purpose with Retreat itself.

question: if an opponent moves unit off of battlefield before akali legend resolves, does the unit still go back to base?
answer:
No — if the unit is no longer in a showdown when Rogue Assassin's ability resolves, the ability's "move to base" instruction is ignored and the unit stays where the opponent's effect put it.

Rogue Assassin's [Action] ability reads "move a friendly unit in a showdown to base." That's the targeting requirement, checked again at resolution (Rule 359.3.e.2). If the opponent's reaction moved the unit off the battlefield (to base, another battlefield, or a non-board zone), the unit is no longer in a showdown, so it becomes an illegal target and the instruction can't be followed (Rule 359.3.e.5). The linked "ready it" (if Empowered) is ignored too (Rule 359.3.e.14.a).

Nuance: if the opponent's effect moved it to base, the unit does end up at base anyway — but that's the opponent's own effect doing that, not the legend. If they moved it elsewhere, it stays there. answer:

The restriction (and the Stunned status) both expire during step 3d of the end-of-turn cleanup — that's when all "this turn" effects expire simultaneously (Rule 317.2.c; CR 424.1.a.2). So your unit stays Stunned and immovable by you for the rest of that turn, regardless of what happens to Vex.

One nuance: the "they" in Vex's text refers to the unit's controller, so it stops you from moving it. If your opponent (or another player) plays an effect that moves your unit, that's not affected — only moves made by the unit's controller are blocked.

question: Can you empower renekton any number of time in risen altar
answer:
No — you can't. Risen Altar only discounts actual Empower keyword costs, and Renekton, Brute doesn't have one — and nothing on either card grants the special permission to become Empowered more than once.

Renekton, Brute's activated ability is "[1]: Give me +1 Might this turn" — that's a pump ability, not an Empower ability (his Keywords line shows Empowered/Deflect/Ganking only).

Even for units that do have Empower, Rule 827.1.c.1 makes it "Play only if not Empowered." Once a unit gains the Empowered status, the ability can't activate again — unless a card text explicitly grants permission to be Empowered multiple times (CR 442.1.c.1). Renekton's "When my Might becomes 10 or more, empower me" fires once when he crosses that threshold for the first time (and only if he wasn't already Empowered — "empower me. I become Empowered if I'm not already"). If he's already at 10+, the "become" event never re-occurs (FAQ #11768).

If you disempower Renekton (e.g., with Profiteer), then yes, you could empower him again later — but that's a separate removal/restoration of the status, not "any number of times" from Risen Altar.

question: Can repeat cost be reduced with applied researcher
answer:
Yes — while Applied Researchers is Empowered, its discount reduces a Repeat cost, but only the one you actually choose to pay.

Repeat is an optional additional cost added to the base cost when you declare it (Rule 820.1), and discounts are applied to that combined total once (Rule 356.4.f — same treatment as Eager Apprentice, FAQ #629). So the Empowered discount — spells cost 1 Energy less (minimum 1) and 1 any-domain Power less — shaves the Repeat cost together with the base cost, not twice. If you don't declare Repeat, there's nothing extra to discount; and if the spell's Energy cost is already at the 1 floor, the Energy part of the discount won't help, though a Power-denominated Repeat (e.g. Repeat [A] or [C]) would still get the [A] Power discount.

question: Applied researcher with deflect and repeat costs
answer:

The Ambush unit was never chosen, so it remains on the battlefield, and since your opponent still has a unit there they keep control and keep their Defender designation (Rule 187.4.c). Control isn't lost just because the bounced unit left — the Ambush unit holds the location for them.

Temporary kills your Sprite at the start of your Beginning Phase before scoring, so the Sprite is already in your trash by the time you hold and Deceiver triggers (Rule 816.1.b; Rule 315.2 — Beginning Step, then Scoring Step). Since the copy effect needs "another unit there," there's no Sprite left to clone.

The only way it works is if the Sprite is created during that same Beginning Phase after the start-of-phase Temporary check (e.g., you make one in response to another Temporary trigger). Then yes — Deceiver fires on your hold, and you get a ready 3/3 Reflection copy you can use the rest of that turn to move or conquer. But that Reflection has Temporary (Deceiver grants it regardless of the copy, and copying the Sprite also carries its keyword), so it dies at the start of your next Beginning Phase — again before scoring. It can never be the unit that "holds" a battlefield at a later Beginning Phase; use it aggressively the same turn.

question: What happens if i cast sanction to empower Kharox and then cast another sanction to disempower it. Do the end of turn effect of each sanction still trigger?
answer:
Yes — both end-of-turn effects still trigger, because each Sanction created its own Delayed Ability that fires on its own schedule regardless of what happened in between (CR 393).

Casting the second Sanction (mode 2, "Disempower... Empower it at end of turn") does not cancel the first Sanction's pending "Disempower it at end of turn." At the Ending Step both delayed triggers go on the chain. Since you control both, you choose their order (Rule 383.3.d).

Sanction #1's delayed disempower: if Kharox is already disempowered when it resolves, it does nothing (CR 443.1.a.1).

Sanction #2's delayed empower: it will still Empower Kharox at end of turn — and since Kharox is no longer Empowered at that point, this is a new Empower event that retriggers his "When I become Empowered" (Burn 3, then optionally play a unit from their trash).

Ordering matters only for the final state: if Sanction #2's empower resolves last, Kharox ends the turn Empowered; if Sanction #1's disempower resolves last, it removes the status. Note Empowered isn't a "this turn" effect, so whichever empowerment survives the Ending Step carries into the next turn.

question: Can Tideturner choose a unit that is already in base and swap location with it?

One catch: if Tideturner is played to your Base (not from Hidden), a unit already at Base is at the same location and cannot be chosen — the target must be at "another location" (FAQ 7937).

question: Will Jayce brilliant inventor trigger on itself and the first non-toke gear played each turn?
answer:
Yes — those are two separate trigger conditions on the same ability, and both can fire in one turn.

Playing Jayce fulfills the "when you play me" clause, and since Jayce is a Unit, not a Gear (Rule 148), that play does not count as — or use up — the "first non-token gear" clause. If you then play your first non-token gear that turn while Jayce is still in play, that clause triggers separately.

So in a clean sequence — play Jayce, then later play your first non-token gear — you may ready once per trigger, up to two different exhausted things (never Jayce himself). Each individual trigger still only readies one thing. Note the gear clause can only fire if the first non-token gear is played after Jayce is on the board; a gear played before he arrives doesn't set it off.

question: Can Zed’s Shadow Clones conquer an open battlefield with zero might? Can it also hold a battlefield alone with zero might?
answer:
Yes to both — a unit's Might has nothing to do with Control, Conquering, or Holding.

A 0-Might Shadow Clone is still a unit (Rule 187.11), and control is established purely by having your units present at a battlefield at the end of a Showdown. If a clone is the only unit at an open battlefield when the Non-Combat Showdown closes, you establish Control and Conquer it for 1 point if you haven't already scored that battlefield this turn (CR 348.2.a, 471.1). Similarly, it can Hold: a clone sitting there alone during your Beginning Phase keeps you in Control and nets the Hold point (CR 190.4.a, 471.2).

The real vulnerability is combat, not Might: in a Combat Showdown the clone adds 0 damage to your pool and dies to any non-zero damage assigned to it (CR 467.2.c.2). And the normal once-per-battlefield-per-turn scoring limit still applies.

question: If Trusty Ramhound is defending at a battlefield with an ally, the ally is assigned lethal damage from the combat resolution, and the Trusty Ramhound is assigned two remaining damage, will Trusty Ramhound live?
answer:
Yes — Trusty Ramhound survives.

Here's why: Trusty Ramhound is Might 3 while its ally is present (base 2 + the +1 Might from its ability). At the combat cleanup's kill check, the game evaluates lethal damage for all units at one point in time while the ally is still alive — so Ramhound has only 2 damage marked against Might 3, which is not lethal. The ally is killed in that same simultaneous event, and then the Combat Special Cleanup's "Heal all Units" step (CR 468.1.a.1) removes Ramhound's 2 damage before any later check can kill it. Even though Ramhound's Might drops to 2 when the ally dies, its damage is already healed.

This matches the established Lee Sin aura rulings (FAQ #5961, #7339) and FAQ #2301: "A unit that would drop to lethal damage after another unit dies will survive if it heals during the cleanup." Note that this only works because healing happens during the same combat cleanup — outside combat (e.g., a kill spell removing the ally), Ramhound would take lethal in the subsequent cleanup.

answer:
Yes — Trusty Ramhound lives.

Combat damage is all dealt at once, and the Combat Cleanup kills lethal-damage units before it heals — but the lethal check happens while the ally is still on the board. Ramhound is at 3 Might (2 base + 1 from the ally), so 2 damage isn't lethal; only the ally dies in the kill step, then Combat Cleanup's "heal all units" removes Ramhound's 2 damage before anything can re-check it (CR 323.4, 468.1.a.1; FAQ #7339/#5961).

A cleaner way to see it: a cleanup can't be interrupted mid-way — nothing between the kill step and the heal step re-evaluates Ramhound's Might. Note the caveat: this survival is specific to combat. If the ally died to spell damage instead, the subsequent non-combat cleanup would have no healing step, and Ramhound would then be killed once its Might dropped to 2 with 2 damage marked (FAQ #7339).

question: In 4 players FFA How meny players can be at the same battlefield while showdown? And how to deal with cards that can create this situation like moonfall and Irresistible Faefolk
answer:
Max is 2 players — combat (and any showdown) only ever involves exactly two players' units in FFA4 (CR 464).

A third player can never have units at the battlefield where a showdown/combat is occurring. That battlefield is an Invalid Destination for their units' moves (CR 449.2.a, 464.1), they can't play units into it (CR 464.2 — they'd go to Base instead), and no unit may move to a battlefield already holding two other players' units "by any means" (CR 451.2). So while other players can cast spells during your showdown (turn order from the attacker), their units cannot be there.

Moonfall and Irresistible Faefolk cannot force a third player into an existing fight. The enemy unit they move is subject to the same destination rules: if it's controlled by a player not involved in the combat who has no units there, the destination is invalid, and the choice itself is "invalid and ineligible to be completed" (CR 464.3). Since both effects are optional ("you may"), you simply move nothing. You can only use them to (a) pull a unit from an enemy who already has units at that battlefield (that unit just becomes the defender), or (b) start a fresh 2-player fight at a battlefield where only you have units — e.g., during someone else's showdown, target a different battlefield you hold; that new fight stages and waits for the current one to finish (FAQ #5108). Moonfall's -2 penalty still hits enemy units there even if you move no one.

Two important caveats:

If the Reflection already finished copying before the original got Star-Crossed/Gusted/killed, it isn't 0 Might at all — a finished copy effect persists, so it keeps the copied unit's Might and text even after the original leaves. The "0 Might Reflection" only exists when the copy was stopped in response (copy target gone before the effect resolved, FAQ #10681).

A Reflection from Mirror Image/Deceiver always ends up with Temporary — the grant isn't tied to the copy succeeding (FAQ #11492). Temporary kills it at the start of its controller's Beginning Phase, before scoring (Rule 816.1.b), so it will die before the Hold scoring step. If it's alone on a battlefield when that happens, you lose Control in the cleanup and get no Hold point — the Reflection can conquer during the window it lives, but it can't be the unit that Holds. (Without Temporary, a 0 Might Reflection would hold fine.)

Combat is where 0 Might hurts: if the battlefield it moves to has enemy units, it adds 0 damage and dies to anything assigned to it — conquering only works against empty/uncontested battlefields.

question: does mel newly awakened when empowered give additional - might when applying switcheroo?
answer:
Yes — an Empowered Mel does add the extra -1 [M], applied to the unit on the losing side of the swap.

Swap isn't a single value-setting action: CR 434.1.a/b says a swap creates two effects — an Increase for the difference on the lower-Might unit and a Decrease of that same amount on the higher-Might unit. That Decrease is a "give -[M]" event to a unit your spell chose (Switcheroo targets both units), so Mel's replacement effect (Rule 370.1) replaces it with a Decrease of one more.

Example: unit A at 5 [M], unit B at 2 [M] at the same battlefield → Switcheroo gives A -3 (Mel makes it -4, so A ends at 1 [M]) and B +3 (B ends at 5 [M]). The swap is therefore no longer a perfect reversal. Only the -[M] side is affected — Mel never touches the Increase.

Edge case: if both units have the same Might, CR 434.1.c says the swap does nothing, so no -[M] event occurs and Mel adds nothing (same logic as the official Stupefy-on-a-1-[M]-unit ruling, FAQ #11759). This all assumes Mel is Empowered and you control the Switcheroo.

question: Can you chain reactions?
answer:
Yes — you can. Once a chain exists the turn is in a Closed State, and only Reaction-speed cards and abilities can be added to it, so any number of Reactions can stack on top of each other (Rule 309.1.a, 813).

They resolve last-in-first-out, and there's a fresh priority window after each item resolves — both players get a chance to add another Reaction before the next item resolves. So you can keep the chain going at every step, not just at the initial play.

One limit: a Reaction is still a Reaction. You can't slip an Action, a unit, or a non-Reaction activated ability onto an existing chain — wait for it to clear.

question: Define hold
answer:
Hold is the scoring method where a player keeps control: you Hold when you maintain Control of a battlefield you have not yet scored this turn, during your Beginning Phase (CR 471.2). It's the passive counterpart to Conquer — Conquer is gaining Control of a battlefield you didn't control; Hold is still controlling one when your turn begins.

When you Hold, you gain up to 1 point (subject to the Final Point restrictions that apply only to Conquer, CR 473.1.a.1), and any "when I hold / when you hold" abilities trigger at the battlefield that was Held (CR 473.2.b) — these are Hold Effects and go on the Chain as Pending Items. Hold happens as part of the Beginning phase of your turn.

One limit matters in practice: you can only score each battlefield once per turn, so a battlefield you already Conquered this turn can't also be Held for a second point (CR 472).

question: What happens if switcheroo is played on forbidding waste where one player the attacker has a 5 might unit and the other has a 1 might unit defending
answer:
They swap — the attacker's unit becomes 1 Might and the defending unit becomes 5 Might, and Forbidding Waste's -2 keeps applying to the defender on top of that.

Switcheroo swaps the units' current Might (CR 434.1.b: take the difference, increase the lower value and decrease the higher), so the battlefield's -2 is already baked into the defender's 1 when the swap is calculated. The -2 then continues to apply afterward, because Forbidding Waste is a passive "while defending alone" effect that re-evaluates continuously — the defender is still defending alone, so nothing falls off (FAQ #10921).

Practical consequence: since damage uses current Might at the Combat Damage Step (CR 467.2), the 1-Might attacker assigns only 1 damage to the 5-Might defender, while the defender assigns 5 to the attacker's unit — almost certainly killing it. Note the swap only lasts this turn.

question: What's the process of playing a gear, how does equip work, when can I play a gear and equip it, where can the unit be when I equip a gear?
answer:
Short version: Play the gear to your Base (it enters ready), then use its Equip ability — an activated ability usable in your Main Phase during an Open State — to attach it to any unit you control, wherever that unit is.

Playing a gear. Pay its cost; it goes on the Chain, finalizes, and resolves immediately — units and gear skip Execute/Pass, so opponents get no reaction window to the play itself (FAQ #8333). By default gear enters your Base, ready (Rules 149.1–149.2), and can be played on your turn in an Open State.

How Equip works. Equip is an Activated Ability: [Cost]: Attach this gear to a unit you control (Rule 818.1.c.2). It behaves like a spell without a card — it goes on the Chain, so the state closes and opponents can respond with Reactions to it (FAQ #9560). Standard timing is your Main Phase, Open State, and not during a Showdown (Rules 151.2, 381) — so it's neither an Action nor a Reaction (FAQ #1120). Once the gear is attached its rules text goes inactive, so you can't use that Equip ability to move it off (Rules 718.2, FAQ #2139); you can still pile multiple gears on one unit (FAQ #6479).

Timing after playing. Yes — you can play a gear and immediately Equip it in the same Main Phase, as long as you have the resources for the Equip cost and the state is Open with no Showdown running. Quick-Draw is the exception: it grants Reaction inherently and auto-attaches on play (Rule 819.1.d), letting you play and attach at Reaction timing.

Where the unit can be. Anywhere you control it — your Base or a Battlefield you control; Equip has no location restriction on the target unit. If you equip a unit at a battlefield, the gear becomes located there through the Attach action (Rule 152.2); if that unit later dies, the gear stays at that battlefield and gets Recalled to your Base at the next Cleanup (CR 459, 149.3).

question: When Switcheroo swaps current Might values between two units, does the Forbidding Waste penalty get counted once in the swap calculation, or does it apply separately on top of the swapped values?
answer:
Counted once — the −2 is part of the unit's current Might when Switcheroo resolves, and it then keeps applying as an ongoing static effect rather than being added a second time.

Switcheroo determines the difference between the two units' current Might (CR 434.1.b), so Forbidding Waste's −2 is already baked into that number and the swap modifier is sized to hit the correct totals. Unlike a spell effect, Forbidding Waste is a passive "while" ability, so it doesn't snapshot — it re-evaluates continuously (CR 479.4.b, FAQ #10921).

Practical result: after the swap the unit at Forbidding Waste still has the −2 applied on top of the fixed swap modifier. Example — lone defender base 4 (currently 2 with the penalty) swaps with a 6 Might unit: the defender ends at 4 − 2 + 4 = 6 and the other unit at 2. If that defender later stops being alone, the −2 vanishes and it jumps to 8, while the swap modifier stays fixed for the turn.

Dragon's ability resolves.

question: if jayce man of progress kills a gold gear token do you get the added power from the gold. if so can i use that power to pay for the vanguard armory that ill also use from his ability
answer:
No, and it matters why — a Gold token killed by Jayce's trigger adds no Power. Jayce's "you may kill a friendly gear" is an "if you do" instruction that happens during his trigger's resolution, not a cost, so it never activates the Gold token's ability. The 1 Power comes only from activating the token's own ability — Kill this, [T]: [Reaction] — Add [A] — where killing and exhausting the token are the costs. A Gold killed by an outside effect just goes to the trash (same one-Gold-one-use logic as the Malzahar ruling).

Yes, that Power can pay for Vanguard Armory — but you need two gear. Kill a different friendly gear for Jayce's trigger, then activate the Gold token's own ability (it has Reaction + Add, so it finalizes and resolves immediately, CR 430.2). The resulting any-domain [A] Power covers Vanguard Armory's 1 Order Power, since Jayce only ignores its 7 Energy cost, not its Power cost.

Sequencing note: if the Gold is your only gear, activating it for Power means Jayce's "if you do" can never be satisfied, and you get no gear play at all. And per the Jayce clarification, the free-ish gear play happens any time after the trigger resolves, still that turn — so rune pool Power you're holding stays usable.

question: If I have a heron on a battlefield and for my first card I discipline my heron but my opponent uses defy and that resolves. Do I still have the discount for the next card?
answer:
No — the discount never triggers, because Discipline was countered and never resolved.

Heron's trigger checks whether your first card completed resolution (CR 420.4.a), and a countered card is not considered played for abilities that trigger on cards being played (CR 426.1.b). Your opponent's Defy resolves first, clearing Discipline off the chain, so no card of yours has resolved and no discount is created. The Defy doesn't count as "your" card either.

If you then play something else this turn and it resolves, that becomes your first card to resolve — Heron fires at that point and the discount applies to the next card you play after it (FAQ #11762).

question: If an opponent uses hidden blade on my unit at a battlefield while pushing in with their unit on the same battlefield, and I draw Rengar, Trophy Hunter from the two cards drawn from Hidden Blade, can I play the Rengar to that battlefield?
answer:
Yes — you can play Rengar there, just not during Hidden Blade's resolution. You can't act mid-resolution, but once Hidden Blade finishes resolving the chain is empty and you get the next Focus window in the still-ongoing Combat Showdown; killing your unit with an action spell in a combat showdown doesn't end the showdown, both players keep getting Action/Reaction windows until both pass consecutively (FAQ #4223).

Rengar's own permission — "I can [Ambush] to a battlefield where there are enemy units, even if you don't have units there" — is an explicit expansion of the normal location rule, so it doesn't matter that your unit died and you now control nothing there; you can play him as a [Reaction] as long as the enemy unit is still present, and he enters as the Defender (Rule 822.1.b; FAQ #9992/#9820).

The only failure case is if no enemy units remain there when you get priority (an open battlefield), in which case he couldn't be played at all (FAQ #11470).

question: Can i play disposal order recycling a card that was being to be chosen by opponent using fizz?
answer:
Yes — as long as you wait until the trigger is actually on the Chain.

Timing is the whole trick: you can't respond to Fizz himself, and you can't preempt the choice. Fizz is played, resolves onto the board, then his "When you play me" ability goes on the Chain and that's when your opponent picks (and locks in) the spell in their trash — targeting happens at finalization, not at resolution (Rule 352.4.b). Now that trigger exists, so you respond to it with Disposal Order (it has [Reaction], so it's legal in the Closed State).

LIFO resolves Disposal Order first — you choose that same spell, its owner recycles it, and Fizz's ability then finds its target gone. The instruction to play it is ignored, so nothing gets played at all. Your opponent doesn't get to swap in a different card.

Note the flip side: if you have to act before Fizz's trigger exists, you're out of luck — you can't name the card you suspect they'll pick.

question: i react with peacekeeper vi during enemy's turn, im defending a battlefield, does peacekeeper vi stun work?
answer:
No — Vi won't stun in that case. Her ability is an Attack Trigger ("When I attack"), which only fires when she gains the Attacker designation (Rule 383.4.e). Played by the defending player, she enters the ongoing combat on your side and gains the Defender designation instead (Rule 323.2.a), so the trigger condition is never met.

To be clear on the comparison: the "yes" rulings for Vi (FAQ #10034, #10437) all involve the unit being Ambushed in by the attacker. A unit joining mid-combat takes the designation matching its controller's side, so the same play from the defender side produces a defender, not an attacker.

You can legally Ambush her there (you control the battlefield you're defending, satisfying Ambush's "battlefield where you control units" requirement, Rule 822.1.b), she just won't stun anything.

question: se attacco eldon e mi fanno una reaction blade fury assegno prima i danni e poi la mia creatura muore o muoio senza assegnare danni
answer:
Nel questo scenario la tua creatura muore senza assegnare i danni perché ogni volta che hai un Combat, la parte prima è un Showdown e solo dopo che chiudete il Showdown potete assegnare i danni.

Allora se nel questo Showdown il tuo avversario gioca Flurry of Blades e questo effetto risolve, ti farà danni primo, c'è un clean up che vede la tua creatura con danni letale e la manda nella tua trash.

Il danno da combattimento si assegna solo nel Combat Damage Step, che si apre dopo che lo Showdown si chiude (cioè dopo che entrambi i giocatori passano Focus in sequenza). Una magia Reaction che risolve durante lo Showdown fa partire un cleanup che uccide le unità con danno letale, quindi l'unità non è più sul campo nel momento dell'assegnazione, e se dell'attacco non resta nessuna unità il Combat Damage Step non avviene proprio (Regola 465.1; FAQ #6476).

L'unico caso in cui la tua unità "muore ma colpisce comunque" è se resta viva fino al Combat Damage Step: lì il danno viene assegnato e poi inflitto simultaneamente, quindi un'unità che riceve danno letale in quel passo infligge lo stesso il suo danno. Quindi: danneggiata ma non uccisa nella Reaction → combatte; uccisa nella Reaction → non combatte.

question:
If I attack with Ezreal Dashing a battlefield occupied by a Scuttle, can opponent react with Rengar Trophy after Scuttle is killed by Ez effet?

And if he reacts to the trigger "When I attack" with Rengar, can I choose him as a target, or I can only select Scuttle?
answer:
Yes on the Rengar window, no on a second trigger.

Rengar's errata'd text ("I can [Ambush] to a battlefield where there are enemy units, even if you don't have units there") lets him be played as a Reaction to that battlefield as long as your Ezreal is still there. So the opponent can respond either while the "When I attack" trigger is still on the chain, or after it resolves and Scuttle dies — the Showdown only closes once all players pass focus in sequence, so they always get a window (Focus stays with you after a trigger chain resolves, Rule 346.1, but you must pass it eventually).

Ezreal will not trigger again. Attack triggers are checked once per combat, when the unit first gains the Attacker designation (Rule 383.4.e.2.a). Rengar arriving mid-combat is just a new Defender in the same combat, not a new combat. (Only if a genuinely separate combat were later staged at that battlefield would Ezreal be the Defender there, and his ability would trigger off defending — once.)

Yes, he can see your hand first. Scuttle Crab's Deathknell is mandatory, so it goes on the chain the moment Scuttle is killed and resolves before the Showdown can close — you're the chosen opponent, so you reveal your hand and the Scuttle's controller may look at your facedown cards this turn. Nothing about that resolution depends on him committing Rengar, so he gets the information before deciding.

Last part: only Scuttle. Targets for a triggered ability are locked in at finalization on the chain (Rule 352.4.b), which happened before Rengar existed at that battlefield, so you cannot point the damage at him — the 3 damage resolves into Scuttle.

question: does star crossed cancel if someone plays temporal breach on a target
answer:
No — Star-Crossed doesn't cancel. It still resolves and returns whichever of its two targets is still legal.

Temporal Breach banishes the unit (moving it to a non-board zone) and then replays it as a new game object, so that unit is no longer the object Star-Crossed chose and becomes an illegal target (Rule 359.3.e.4). But the other target — whichever of the friendly/enemy pair wasn't Breached — is still on the board, and per Rule 359.3.e.8 the spell executes "as much as possible," returning that unit to its owner's hand (FAQ #10821).

One note: because Temporal Breach's unit re-enters as a fresh object, it won't be the one returned to hand even though it's back at the same location.

question: if elder is played from temporal breach and then enemy reacts flash, does that dodge the elder dragon
answer:
Yes — assuming nothing is already damaged lethally, Flash saves the units.

Elder Dragon's "when you play me" ability is a set of location-based targeting restrictions ("up to one enemy unit at each location"), and each target is checked against its own restriction as the ability resolves. Because the Dragon was played via Temporal Breach, it enters and its passive goes active immediately, but its play trigger is placed on the chain after Temporal Breach finishes resolving, so the opponent does get priority and can Flash before the trigger resolves — moving the units to base means they no longer satisfy the restriction for the location they were chosen at, so they take no damage (FAQ 9919).

The one exception: if a unit already has any damage marked on it by Elder Dragon's controller, the passive makes that lethal, and the cleanup before priority is passed kills it before Flash can ever be played (FAQ 12271). Note the moved units don't get picked up by the base instruction — that instruction locked in its own target at finalization.

question: if karthus is killed first in bellows and then 2nd bellows retrigger targets someone else with deathknell does that karthus still proc it
answer:
Yes — the second unit's Deathknell still triggers an extra time.

Bellows Breath's Repeat executes the whole effect a second time during the same resolution (Rule 820.1.d), and Bellows Breath resolves fully before any cleanup. Karthus has lethal damage marked but hasn't been moved to the trash yet, so he's still on the board and his passive ("Your [Deathknell] effects trigger an additional time") is still applying when the second unit's Deathknell trigger is created. In fact it would work even if both deaths were truly simultaneous (FAQ #10742 / #5353) — passive abilities don't need to survive their own death.

The contrast case: if Karthus had been killed and trashed by a separate, earlier spell or ability (with a cleanup already resolved in between), his passive is gone and the later Deathknell would only trigger once. New choices for the repeated execution — including a different unit — are legal (Rule 820.2.a).

question: If akali moves to a BF and does 2 dmg. then leaves and does 2dmg. but it does not kill the unit. does the unit heal?
answer:
Yes — the unit heals, because a Combat Showdown was opened.

Since there was an enemy unit at that battlefield, Akali's arrival staged a Combat Showdown, and Combat Cleanup heals all Units in play regardless of whether the damage was lethal or whether the unit actually fought (CR 468.1.a). Akali's "When I move" damage is just marked damage, not a kill — so it gets wiped at the end of that combat unless it killed the unit. Pulling her back with Rogue Assassin doesn't dodge this: the legend can only be activated at Action speed, meaning the Showdown is already running and will still clean up (FAQ #11658, #11899).

The one exception is if she's pulled out before the Showdown ever opens — i.e. moving her back at Reaction speed in response to her own move trigger while the chain is still non-empty (like a Flash), so no Combat was ever staged. In that case no Combat Cleanup occurs and the 4 damage stays marked (FAQ #11658). With the legend, that window doesn't exist.

question: Can I use fiora worthy ability in an active showdown
answer:
Yes — but only if its trigger condition happens during that showdown.

Fiora, Worthy's "When a unit you control becomes [Mighty], you may pay [C] to ready it" is a triggered ability, not an activated one, so it isn't blocked by the rule that keeps regular activated abilities out of showdowns (Rule 145.2, 381). When a unit you control actually becomes Mighty (hits 5+ Might, including from a mid-showdown buff or a defender's +1), the ability goes on the chain and can be responded to; the [C] is paid as it resolves, and the ready happens then. If nobody became Mighty — for example Fiora was already Mighty before the showdown started — there's no trigger to use.

See FAQ 6927 for the same sequence: a unit becomes Mighty mid-showdown, Fiora's ability is used, cost paid, unit readied.

question: Can i use trigger ability in a showdown?
answer:
Yes — triggered abilities aren't "activated," so they work during a showdown. A trigger fires automatically when its condition is met and goes on the chain as a Pending Item, and Rule 383.3.c allows that during Closed or Open states on any player's turn, showdown or not.

The key distinction is what the ability is. If it starts with "When…", "At…", or "The Nth time…", it's a triggered ability and it triggers during a showdown just fine. If it's written as [Cost]: [Effect], that's an activated ability, and by default it can only be used on your turn, in a Neutral Open state, out of showdown (Rule 381) — so it can't be used in a showdown unless the card grants it Action or Reaction.

One caveat: if a spell you want to play in response has to be Reaction once the trigger starts a chain — a trigger that opens a chain puts the state in Showdown Closed, where only Reaction-speed plays are legal.

question: Can i use trigger ability's multiple times

It depends on the trigger — triggered abilities are by definition repeatable, but several things cap them.

Normally a triggered ability fires every time its condition is met (Rule 383), so if the condition genuinely happens twice, you get the effect twice. But watch these caps: abilities that say "once each turn" or "the first time…" only fire that many times (Rule 383.3.e), Attack and Defend triggers only fire once per combat even if the unit gains the designation again in that same combat (Rules 383.4.e.2.a / 383.4.f.2.a), and Conquer triggers need an actual Conquer — since each battlefield can only be scored once per turn, you can't re-conquer it to farm the trigger.

question: Can I use Fiora worthy ability in combat?
answer:
Yes — Fiora, Worthy's ability is a triggered ability ("When a unit you control becomes [Mighty]…"), so it can go on the chain during a Combat Showdown.

The Main Phase / Open State restriction (Rule 381) applies only to activated abilities. Triggered abilities fire whenever their condition is met, including mid-combat — e.g., a unit reaching 5 Might from a buff, a Might pump, or Shield kicking in when it's declared as a defender. Resolving it during combat is fine; you just pay the [C] and ready the unit.

Two caveats: the trigger only sees an actual in-play Might change to 5+, so a unit that enters play already at 5+ Might won't trigger it (Rule 709 / FAQ #5835); and like any trigger it uses the chain, so opponents get priority in response.

question:
If I have a void hatchling on the board and play double trouble or ivern which say:
look at the top 3 cards you may reveal a unit...

Does the void hatching trigger at all?
answer:
Short answer: Void Hatchling doesn't "trigger" at all — it's a replacement effect, not a triggered ability — and it hooks onto the reveal part of Double Trouble / Ivern, Nurturer, not the "look at the top 3."

The look-at-3 is a look, not a reveal, so Hatchling has nothing to apply to there — same reasoning as Stacked Deck (FAQ #1404). But both of those cards then instruct you to reveal a unit from your deck, and that's the instruction Hatchling replaces: you look at the top card of your deck first (which will be one of the three you're already looking at), you may recycle it, and then you reveal a unit from among the looked-at cards and draw it.

Practically, that's a small upgrade — you get to bottom the top card before making your choice instead of having it swept up in "recycle the rest" afterward — and note if you recycle the card that was your unit, it's gone before the reveal happens.

One caveat: FAQ #766/#1404 establish the look-vs-reveal split and that Hatchling replaces rather than triggers, but I didn't find a published Q&A that runs it against Double Trouble/Ivern specifically; the above is the Rek'Sai precedent (FAQ #315) applied to these cards.

question: When opponent's warwick enter and I have emperor divide in hand. Can I use emperor divide from my hand to escape warwick kill ability?
answer:
No — not from hand. Emperor's Divide in hand is only an [Action] spell, and once Warwick's attack trigger goes on the chain the turn is in a Closed State, where only [Reaction] cards can be played (Rule 309.1.a). Warwick's "when I attack, kill all damaged enemy units here" trigger is added to the initial chain of combat, so your only window there is reaction speed.

Note there's also no window earlier: playing Warwick gives no reaction opportunity (permanents auto-resolve), and he's already an attacker with the trigger on the chain by the time a showdown opens, so you never get an Open State to play the Action before the kill resolves.

If you had hidden Emperor's Divide earlier at a battlefield you control, it would work — from Hidden it gains Reaction and plays for [0], so you could respond, moving your damaged units to Base; they're no longer "here" when Warwick's trigger resolves and so survive (same logic as FAQ #3645).

question: I move my Akali - Deadly weapon into a battlefield solely with oponent's Akali - Silent. Do I deal damage? If I react to my Akali move trigger with flash, does it deal any damage? If instead I use Akali, Rogue Assassin ability, does it deal any damage?
answer:
No for the first two, yes for the third — it all turns on whether Akali, Silent is "in combat" (i.e. holds an Attacker/Defender designation) at the moment your move trigger's target is chosen.

Straight move in: no damage. Your "When I move" trigger is finalized — targets picked — the instant she arrives, and a Combat Showdown only opens during a Cleanup with an empty Chain (CR 462), so Akali, Silent has no Defender designation yet and isn't "in combat." She's Untargetable to your ability, so you can't choose her and nothing is dealt (cf. FAQ #12466, #11816).

Flash in response: still no damage. Flash sends her back to base and adds a second "When I move" trigger (the battlefield she moved from), but the Chain never empties, so no Showdown ever opens and Akali, Silent never gains a designation — neither trigger can choose her. This is the opposite of the usual Akali Flash trick, which only works because a normal unit is targetable (FAQ #11658).

Rogue Assassin legend: yes, 1 damage (2 if Empowered) — but it's healed after the showdown will close. You can only activate the legend once the Showdown has actually started, which means it's already a Combat Showdown and Akali, Silent is the Defender (CR 466.2.c.3 — designations persist until combat ends, CR 468.7.a). She is in combat, so choosable, and the pull-back trigger hits her. If all players then pass their focus you will go directly to a combat cleanup as there will be no attackers that could assign damage to defenders and vice versa and a Combat Cleanup then heals every unit in play, so unless the damage was lethal she ends at full health (FAQ #12550).

question: Does the Harrowing banish a unit before playing it? Does it empowers Zed legend?
answer:
No — The Harrowing never banishes anything. Its text is just "Play a unit from your trash, ignoring its Energy cost," so the chosen unit moves trash → chain → board as a new game object; banishment is only involved when an effect explicitly says "banish" (Arcane Shift, Portal Rescue).

Two things that follow from that: since it's a play and not a banish, it's not a "banished" event for any trigger, and it does target the card in your trash when the spell finalizes, so an opponent can react with something like Disposal Order to remove it first (FAQ #12258, Rule 359.3.e).

question: If a flow card is in trash, and you conquer with Kennen, can I play using kennen’s flow cost instead?
answer:
Yes — you choose. Both the printed Flow cost and Kennen's granted Flow cost become instances of Flow on the same spell, and the controller picks which one to apply when playing it (Rule 829.1.c.3).

Worth knowing: Kennen's granted cost is "equal to its cost," which is checked against the spell's printed cost (CR 206) — so it's usually the base cost, and for most Flow spells (e.g. Shadow Dash at [5][A][A]) Kennen's grant is the cheaper option. You're never forced to use it; if the printed Flow cost is lower, take that one.

Two timing notes: the grant only lasts that turn, and Kennen's "When I conquer" trigger resolves as the showdown closes/control is established, so there's no showdown window left at that instant (FAQ #12519) — you need a later legal window that same turn (a Showdown for an Action spell, or any priority if the spell has Reaction if these happen on your opponents turn or during your turn when the turn is in the Neutral Open state, which is when no Chain exists and there is no Showdown active). Either way, playing it from trash banishes it after it resolves.

question: When Kennen, Keeper of Balance is played from Ava Achiever's ability, does Kennen's ability trigger twice, from being played and from attacking?
answer:
Yes — you get two separate instances of the ability, one for each condition met.

Kennen's "When you play me or I attack" is a single triggered ability but with two distinct trigger events, and it has no "once each turn" limit, so each fulfilled condition puts its own instance on the chain. The "when you play me" instance is placed when Kennen enters (Rule 383.4.a.2); because Ava plays him "here" into the battlefield where her combat is ongoing, he then gains the Attacker designation during the next Cleanup along with his controller (Rule 323.2.a), which places the attack-trigger instance (Rule 383.4.e.2). Arriving late to a combat still counts — that's the same principle as FAQ #4095/#716.

Each instance is a separate "you may pay [2] to stun a unit," so you decide independently for each: pay for one, both, or neither, and you choose the order if they're placed simultaneously (Rule 383.3.d). Note Ava plays him from hand, not from Hidden, so neither stun is restricted to targeting units at his battlefield. If he's played somewhere he never becomes an attacker (e.g.: base, if Ava's moved to base before her trigger resolves), you get only the single play trigger.

question: How would this interaction work if I had a Viktor, Leader on the board? I play a Jayce, Man of Progress using his ability to target and kill a Patched Porobot on my board to play another gear from my hand. Because Patched Porobot is both a gear and a unit would killing it trigger Viktor, Leader and let me play a Recruit unit token?
answer:
Yes — Viktor, Leader triggers and you get a 1 Might Recruit token.

Patched Porobot is both a Unit and a Gear, and per the multiple-types rules it keeps all the properties of both (Rule 178.1). Jayce's "kill a friendly gear" instruction resolves and sends Porobot to the trash from the board — that's a kill, so the permanent's death is a unit's death. Since Porobot is a non-Recruit unit you control, Viktor's "when another non-Recruit unit you control dies" condition is satisfied, and Viktor is still on the board to see it (no simultaneity problem here, unlike Viktor dying alongside another unit).

Timing: Viktor's trigger is placed on the chain as a pending item while Jayce's play effect is resolving, so it finalizes and resolves after Jayce's ability finishes — you play the Recruit token into your base, and you can still play the gear from hand any time later that turn (per the Jayce clarification).

One note: the Recruit token itself won't re-trigger Viktor, since Recruits are excluded from his condition.

question: does killing a gold gear token activate the sivir battle mistress legend ability?
answer:
No. Sivir, Battle Mistress (Battle Mistress) has exactly two triggers: "When you recycle a rune, you may exhaust me to play a Gold gear token exhausted" and "When one or more enemy units die, ready me." Killing a Gold gear token satisfies neither.

A Gold token is a gear, not a unit (Rule 187.5), so its death never counts as "an enemy unit dies." And killing a gear is not recycling a rune — recycling is a specific action that moves a rune back into your rune deck, not a Kill (CR 429). Note also that when you kill the Gold via its own ability ("Kill this, [E]: [Add] [A]"), the kill is a cost, not a recycle, so nothing about that sequence touches Sivir.

So the only ways to fire Sivir are a genuine rune recycle (for the Gold token trigger) or an enemy unit actually dying (for the ready trigger).

question: does using a gold gear token activate the sivir battle mistress legend ability of "when you recycle a rune"?
answer:
No. Exhausting and killing a Gold gear token just adds one Power to your Rune Pool — it isn't a Recycle action, so Sivir's "when you recycle a rune" trigger never fires.

Gold's activated ability is "Kill this, [E]: [Reaction] — Add [A]," which generates Power rather than returning a rune to your Rune Deck (FAQ 9224). Recycling, by contrast, is specifically moving a card to the bottom of its deck — runes go to the Rune Deck (CR 417.1.b).

So Sivir only triggers off a real recycle event (for example, a basic Rune's "Recycle this: [Reaction] — Add [C]"). Notably, the Gold token Sivir makes is what you'd later cash in for Power — it doesn't loop back into triggering her.

question: After playing a unit with Glasc Mixologist Deathknell, does the HP reset?
answer:
Yes — the unit you play from the trash enters with no damage marked on it, and any damage on your surviving units was already healed before the trigger resolved.

Damage doesn't persist on cards in the trash, so the new unit enters fresh. And in the standard case (Mixologist dying in a Combat Showdown), Combat Cleanup heals every unit in play before the Deathknell trigger is finalized and resolved, so you can't use the trigger to "finish off" an enemy that survived combat — they're already healed to full by the time your unit arrives (CR 463.1.a.1). This is also why Mixologist's Deathknell can't save a unit that already took lethal damage.

One caveat: the automatic heal only comes from Combat Cleanup (or the end-of-turn heal). If Mixologist is killed outside combat, nothing is auto-healed — but the newly played unit still enters with zero damage either way.

question: Can I star Crossed a sprite token in the beginning phase by reacting to its own temporary trigger?
answer:
Yes, the timing works — but Star-Crossed needs two targets, so it often can't be cast at all in that spot.

Temporary is a triggered ability that goes on the chain at the start of its controller's Beginning Phase, which creates a Closed State, and Star-Crossed's [Reaction] lets you play it there (Rules 816, 813). Confirmed by FAQ #6571/#5523, which allow reacting to a Sprite's Temporary trigger. However, Star-Crossed requires both a friendly unit and an enemy unit as targets — if the Sprite is your only unit, or your opponent controls no units, you have no legal cast.

Note that bouncing your own Sprite doesn't save it: the token goes to hand and immediately ceases to exist (Rule 186.1), so it leaves play just the same. The difference is it isn't "Killed" — so any Kill/Deathknell-style triggers won't fire, and the Temporary trigger resolves afterward with nothing left to kill.

question: Are there are Order or Law cards that allows me to play cards more than once, from the grave, or send back to my hand
answer:
Yes, but not many — and there's no "Law" domain in Riftbound (the domains are Order, Chaos, Calm, Body, Mind, Fury; "Keeper of Law" is simply an Order card).

For playing out of the trash, Order has Spectral Matron, Glasc Mixologist (on Deathknell), and the spell Undying Loyalty — each plays a unit from your trash ignoring its cost. Order also carries the Flow keyword (Dragon Form, Lacerate, Shadow Dash, Public Execution, Lightning Rush); Flow is a permission plus alternate cost that lets you play that same spell from your trash once, then it's banished — that's the main "play a card more than once" mechanic in these colors.

For returning cards to hand, Starhound is the only Order hit, and it's narrow: it returns a Bird, Cat, Dog, or Poro from your trash to hand. Order has no board-to-hand bounce, and Forge of the Future recycles up to 4 cards from trashes back into the deck (not your hand). Nothing in Order (or anywhere) loops a card back repeatedly for free.

question: Do heron ability starts a chain?
answer:
Yes — Astral Heron's ability is a triggered ability ("When you play your first card each turn…"), and all triggered abilities are placed on the Chain as a Pending Item, which creates a Closed State where opponents can respond with [Reaction] cards (Rule 383.3).

Two practical notes: its "if I'm at a battlefield" clause is checked when the trigger fires, not when it resolves, so bouncing or killing the Heron in response does not stop the discount (FAQ #12385). And the discount it creates applies to the next card you play after the ability resolves — it won't retroactively discount a card already on the Chain.

question: When using Hostile Takeover on a tapped Irelia Fervent, does Irelia get +1 from the ready?
answer:
Yes — she gets the +1. Hostile Takeover resolves its instructions in order (take control, then ready), so by the moment the unit is readied, you are already her controller. Irelia's "when you choose or ready me" is read from the perspective of her controller (CR 191.5.a), so the readied-by-you clause is satisfied even though you're taking her from an opponent.

Worth distinguishing from FAQ #236's note that an opponent readying Irelia doesn't trigger her: there the opponent never gains control of her, so the "you" never applies. Here the control change lands first.

Two notes: if she were already ready, nothing would happen (CR 416.1.b/c, a ready unit can't be readied again), and Hostile Takeover also targets her, so you'd typically net +2 Might for the turn (+1 chosen, +1 readied) — the ready trigger is placed on the chain after the spell finishes resolving.

question: I was using OGS-019 Master Yi, and I had a Pouty Poro on a battlefield. Enemy had a Ravenbloom Student and an Eager Apprentice in the base. It was the enemy’s turn. He moved the Apprentice to my battlefield and started a combat showdown. He started a chain with Smoke Screen targeting my Poro. I passed and let it resolve. Then I started a chain with Discipline and it resolved. He passed focus and I casted Rune Prison on his Apprentice, he reacted with a Stupefy on my Poro. And the showdown ended with no unit died, and the Apprentice was sent back to the base. He then attacked with the Ravenbloom student. What should be the might of my Poro at this point?
answer:
Your Poro is 2 Might when it defends against the Ravenbloom Student.

The key is what Smoke Screen saw when it resolved. By then the Apprentice had already moved in and the combat showdown had started, so your Poro was the lone defender and Wuju Bladesman's "defending alone" passive was live — its Might was 2 + 2 = 4. Smoke Screen's -4 is clamped by its "minimum of 1" clause and snapshots at that moment, so it locks in as -3 for the turn, not -4 (CR 479.4.b; increases apply before decreases, FAQ #1455).

After that: Discipline +2, then Stupefy -1 (applied unclamped, since the Poro was at 3 then). So when the Student attacks: 2 base + 2 (defending alone) − 3 (Smoke Screen) + 2 (Discipline) − 1 (Stupefy) = 2 Might.

Worth flagging the trap: if you'd let Smoke Screen resolve before the Apprentice moved (as in the classic Watcher/Stalwart Poro line), it would have snapshotted at only -1 and your Poro would be 4 here. Because it resolved mid-showdown, you take the -3.
